Our research analyzed 143 days of data from the ASgamma dataset at energies above 4 EeV. We found a dipole anisotropy at (1.22 +/- 0.17) x 10^-3 cosine with theta_z = 179 degrees, which increased to (4.2 +/- 0.8) x 10^-3 cosine with theta_z = 112 degrees when considering only energies above 4 EeV without magnetic vector dependence. We also discovered quadrupole anisotropies at energies above 4 EeV with strengths (4.0 +/- 1.5) x 10^-6, (6.2 +/- 2.1) x 10^-7, and -2.0 +/- 1.3) x 10^-6 in lambda, phi, and lambda^2*phi respectively, exhibiting an energy dependent pattern similar to the amplitude of the dipole anisotropy. However, our findings differ slightly from previous results due to a broader definition of quadrupole components. Additionally, we observed an increase in anisotropy amplitude from 4-10 EeV and 4-20 EeV, and a directional shift from 11-20 EeV, suggesting a feature at the knee of the energy spectrum and a global pattern. We also discovered an energy and direction dependent octupole anisotropy, which may be caused by local and global features, and recommend further research with extended exposure and finer energy resolution. We've developed a formalism for noncommutative quantum mechanics based on differential operators in a commuting momentum space. This approach allows us to generalize classical Poisson brackets to noncommutative ones, denoted as $\{x^i,x^j\}_\star$. Our expression for $\{x^i,x^j\}_\star$ takes the form $i[\hat{p}_i,\hat{x}_j]_+$, where $[\,\ ]_+$ represents the commutator of operators in the position space. This results in noncommutative Hamiltonian mechanics being governed by an equation resembling $i\dot{\phi}=H_\star$, with $\phi$ encompassing both position and momentum parameters. We've also established a Hamiltonian formulation for noncommutative Chern-Simons theory in this new framework. This involves expressing the time-dependent Chern-Simon Hamiltonian in terms of $\{x^i,x^j\}_\star$. Consequently, we've derived an equation that reflects the noncommutative nature, effectively transforming it into a commutative problem in the momentum space. This has allowed us to successfully reproduce previous studies attaining exact results. Moreover, our work opens up possibilities for exploring other noncommutative field theories utilizing this novel framework. This is the first report on a broader research effort, with additional findings included in the accompanying papers. This initiative is part of the research projects described in [1] and [2]. Precise quantitative insights into the behavior of the immune system are crucial for understanding cancer progression. This knowledge can be gained by examining the levels and types of lymphocytes present in tumors. However, obtaining accurate measurements of these cells on a digitized tissue section requires a manual and time-consuming process. To streamline this measurement process, a novel algorithm has been developed to automatically identify and count lymphocytes within tissue samples. This novel approach uses a deep learning technique called U-Net, with minor adjustments to enhance its performance when working with limited data sets. The developed algorithm was tested on a collection of digitized tissue sections featuring various cancer types and locations, and its results were compared to measurements obtained by cancer experts. The comparison revealed that the accuracy of the algorithm surpasses that of conventional methods and serves as a reliable substitute for conventional methods such as manual counting and the application of shape descriptors in situations where processing speed is a concern. Moreover, the algorithm's efficiency allows for the measurement of lymphocytes at a single cell level, making it an effective solution for analyzing the immune response in cancer research. The algorithm has been made publicly accessible through a user-friendly web server that enables users to upload their own tissue samples for measurement. The algorithm's source code is also available on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. This novel algorithm paves the way for the comprehensive study of the immune response in cancer, which is a crucial step towards a deeper understanding of cancer progression. This understanding is, in turn, a key component in the development of tailored cancer treatment plans. This research is part of the authors' broader endeavor to advance the computational analysis of tumor pathologies through the integration of algorithms, medicine, and computing. This endeavor aims to provide free access to the developed algorithms and their results via straightforward APIs and web servers, facilitating the seamless collaboration of computer scientists and cancer experts worldwide. This approach has the potential to give rise to a comprehensive, open, and publicly accessible cancer pathology repository, contributing significantly to the advancement of cancer research. To mitigate burst errors in high-speed optical communications, we integrate the Weakly Expanding Decision Feedback Equalizer and Maximum Likelihood Sequence Estimator into a single, hybrid system. By simultaneously utilizing the decision feedback equalizer and maximum likelihood detector, this approach enhances the detection of sequence symbols and the performance of burst error resistance. Numerical simulations demonstrate that when confronted with a channel subject to mode discontinuity, the combined WDFE-MLSE method surpasses conventional FDE, MLSE, and WDFE techniques in terms of burst error rate. Additionally, when faced with coherent crosstalk from an adjacent channel, the proposed WDFE-MLSE method outperforms conventional FDE, MLSE, and WDFE methods by a margin of up to 3.2 dB in symbol error rate, and up to 2.5 dB in burst error rate. Moreover, the proposed method achieves a 12.5% improvement in data transfer rate when confronted with a mode-discontinuous channel, and provides a 2.5 dB gain in signal-to-noise ratio when faced with coherent crosstalk from an adjacent channel. Furthermore, the combined WDFE-MLSE method exhibits enhanced sequence estimation accuracy, up to 86.8%, when compared to the conventional MLSE method. The proposed WDFE-MLSE method can be applied to advanced optical communication systems that utilize high-speed digital equalizers, such as coherent optical transmission systems. The method's enhanced performance in the presence of burst errors makes it suitable for high-speed data transfer applications. This project introduces a novel module called Dilated Encoder Module, which achieves both compactness and swiftness in Temporal Convolutional Networks. We analyze the inherent layering pattern in Dilated ENCODE and uncover a hidden repeating module within the network. By extracting this hidden pattern, we successfully apply the Dilated Encoder Module across multiple temporal scales, ultimately generalizing it to any given scale. Utilizing this generalized form, we successfully derived an efficient compiler for TCNs that automates the process of introducing automatic dilation. Our innovations lead to a significant reduction in model size and inference latency, outperforming existing techniques while matching the accuracy. The devised compiler further enables the incorporation of adaptable dilation weights, enhancing TCNs' capability even further. Through thorough experimentation on diverse datasets across multiple tasks, our developed Dilated Encoder Module and automatic dilation optimizer consistently produce results that match or surpass the current state-of-the-art models. We establish that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over an algebraically closed field possesses a nilpotent or solvable characteristic, corroborating a hypothesis initially proposed by Zelmanov. This conviction is supported by an exploration of the properties of Zinbiel central automorphism algebras and their connection to forms of Zinbiel algebras and their relatives, Lie algebras and Jordan algebras. Furthermore, our investigation reveals that a finite-dimensional simple Zinbiel algebra cannot be isomorphic to a Lie algebra or Jordan algebra. We also prove the characteristic of a finite-dimensional solvable Zinbiel algebra to be nilpotent and demonstrate that a nilpotent characteristic of a finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra guarantees the solvability of that algebra. Additionally, we identify an instance of a finite-dimensional nilpotent Zinbiel algebra whose characteristic is not solvable. We conclude with the analysis of power series and their application to constructing new examples of finite-dimensional nilpotent Zinbiel algebras. These constructed algebras serve as models for a broader class of algebras and provide evidence in support of Zelmanov's initial proposal.

Understanding the relationship between the quark-gluon plasma's macroscopic behavior and microscopic motion is crucial for uncovering the underlying dynamics of this system. This study examines the connection between the entanglement thickness of the plasma and the probability distribution of the fluid's velocity field as measured in lead-lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Our analysis indicates that the bulk viscosity, which hinders the velocity field's oscillations, is significantly influenced by the entanglement thickness and temperature at which the entanglement changes to a more viscous state. Notably, our findings also reveal a relationship between the Gaussian-like shape of the probability distribution of energy density fluctuations and entanglement properties. Additionally, our results suggest that the entanglement thickness acts as a mediator between the hydrodynamic response and density fluctuations, yielding a relationship that is largely independent of the hydrodynamic response time. This understanding is anticipated to advance our knowledge of the interplay between microscopically entangled fields and macroscopically hydrodynamically behaving components in quantum systems. Moreover, our analysis could pave the way for further exploring the connections between entanglement and hydrodynamics in diverse systems, including lattice gauge theory, quantum field theories, and possibly even cosmic strings and fundamental string theories. By examining the probability distribution of the fluid velocity field in multiple directions, we are able to simulate publicly available data, thereby validating our approach. Our study's key findings are also shown to hold for distinct initial conditions, indicating that the observed relationships are robust. Finally, we propose that researchers experimentally verify our predictions through the analysis of data from lead-lead and lead-gold collisions at the LHC. Ultimately, this work is expected to contribute to a deeper comprehension of the quark-gluon plasma's fundamental characteristics and its collective behavior in high-energy nuclear experiments. We introduce ALBA, an algorithm for calculating first-order correspondents in LE- and DL-extended inductive formulas, building on the ideas presented in the BEAM and FEME frameworks. ALBA addresses the limitations of these previous approaches and offers a more efficient and user-friendly method for computing first-order correspondents. The ALBA algorithm is capable of determining whether a given formula has a first-order correspondent and can provide a corresponding instance of that formula if one exists. Additionally, ALBA offers two different operation modes, with the option to derive the corresponding instance directly or to arrive at the corresponding instance through a sequence of inherited clauses. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the ALBA algorithm through a set of practical applications and showcase its performance by conducting a series of experiments in various reasoning tasks. The source code for the ALBA algorithm is available online and can be executed on the CAFRI platform. We also present an updated version of the ALBA algorithm, with improvements aimed at reducing the memory consumption and execution time for complex input data. A comparison of the optimized and original versions of the ALBA algorithm is presented in the experimental results. We have incorporated the optimized version of the ALBA algorithm into the CAFRI solver and the CAFRI-BEAM solver, with the source code and further details available online. The optimized version of the ALBA algorithm offers superior performance and efficiency when computing first-order correspondents in LE- and DL-extended inductive formulas, with notable improvements in specific domains and with extended knowledge bases. The optimized ALBA algorithm demonstrates the effectiveness of the original algorithm's underlying methodology and underscores the significance of the algorithm in the context of LE- and DL-extended inductive logic programming. We introduce the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model as an innovative adaptation of the Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (PARX) model. The original PARX model is an advanced variation of the Poisson AutoRegressive model, which utilizes external factors to influence the Poisson process while maintaining its non-negative integer value. However, real-world data often exhibits nonlinear dynamics and sudden changes, or structural breaks, which the TV-PARX model addresses by incorporating a time-varying component into its parameters. We propose an efficient method for estimating the TV-PARX model parameters through the Minimum Contrast Estimation (MCE) algorithm and establish the asymptotic distribution of the estimated parameters. Moreover, we evaluate the performance of the MCE method through simulated data and real-world examples, demonstrating its effectiveness and simplicity. Finally, we explore the TV-PARX model's flexibility by applying the MCE method to count time series with various break points and nonlinear patterns. One such example involves analyzing non-farm payroll employment change data from the US, and another example involves examining the frequency of search engine rankings for a list of keywords. Lastly, we outline several potential future research directions for the TV-PARX model. We make the MCE algorithm code publicly available for the benefit of researchers and practitioners. Inspired by human manipulation, we introduce a novel approach using Neural Descriptor Fields. This method leverages a physical sensor simulator and kinesthetic teaching tool to learn from limited demonstrations. By defining manipulation tasks as optimizing an object configuration according to sensory input, we utilize Neural Descriptor Fields to parameterize objects and their configurations. Our approach extracts task-specific spatial relationships from demonstrations, combining a sensor simulator-based loss with a neural network that identifies distinctive sensory features. This system is demonstrated by teaching a robot to place a cup on a table using a camera, and it successfully generalizes to various starting positions and orientations. When given just one demonstration, it places the cup correctly 95% of the time. Our method extends beyond simple placement tasks, as seen in our supplementary video showing more complex demonstrations. This work will be presented at the 2023 Conference on Robot Learning. The SiD detector, a highly versatile and radiation-resistant particle finder suited for the search for beyond-Standard-Model physics at the ILC, has a highly precise and adaptable calorimeter system that enables it to achieve jet energy resolution of $\sigma_{\rm E}\approx 0.07E^{\rm missing}$ in 3 TeV collisions. This paper provides a detailed description of the design and calculated performance of the SiD calorimeter system, consisting of a highly sensitive and finely granulated component called the hadron calorimeter and a less dense, less granular component called the iron extended component used to measure the energy of muons. The hadron calorimeter, with its high energy resolution and ability to simulate the energy signature of disappearing particles, plays a crucial role in the SiD detector's capability to detect new physics at the ILC. The design and calculated performance of the SiD detector's calorimeter system make it an ideal choice for identifying jet energy signature in 3 TeV collisions, thereby enabling the detection of various particles such as dark photons, axions, and supersymmetric particles. The design also minimizes systematic uncertainties associated with energy measurement, achieving an accuracy of $\pm 1\%$ in energy calibration. The design and calculated performance of the SiD detector's calorimeter system have been validated through various simulations and testing methods, including software simulations and physical prototypes. The calculated performance of the SiD detector's calorimeter system have demonstrated its capability to detect a signal with an energy threshold of 0.3 TeV in 500 GeV collisions, thereby indicating its potential as a reliable particle finder for the ILC. The design and calculated performance of the SiD detector's calorimeter system have also been compared with that of other detector designs, showcasing its innovative features and versatility. The development of the SiD detector's calorimeter system has been accompanied by significant technological advancements, including the introduction of a new compensation material called 'plastic-iron', a lightweight and highly sensitive cooling system, and a cutting-edge high-voltage drift technology. A detailed analysis of the metal-rich globular cluster Tononzintla 2, located in the galaxy NGC 4437, has provided significant insights into the characteristics of this cluster's chemical composition. Based on a comprehensive study of 705 turnoff and red-giant branch stars within the cluster, researchers discovered a high degree of abundance variation, with metal content ranging from $\sim$0.088 to $-$0.024 in Tononzintla 2. Furthermore, a comparison with nineteen other high-metallicity clusters within the Milky Way revealed that the abundance of alpha-elements in this cluster exceeds the universal average, while the abundance of iron is marginally above the typical value observed in high-metallicity clusters. Additionally, Tononzintla 2 exhibits a unique abundance pattern, with a significant abundance of elements with mass numbers greater than 40, which is consistent with a previous finding reported by Soto Minaya et. al. Based on isochrone analysis, a well-defined turnoff point, and a lack of multiple populations as indicated by a narrow CB ratio distribution ranging from 1.01 to 0.85, the age of Tononzintla 2 was estimated to be approximately 10.8 billion years. This age, coupled with the presence of blue horizontal branch stars, places the cluster in the SGB region of the diagram. Recent advancements in metasurfaces have been substantial, with researchers developing a range of strategies to design complex structures using generalized sheet transition conditions. To further expand on this work, this paper proposes an alternative approach, incorporating the differential form version of electromagnetic duality, space-time duality, and the GSTCs. By leveraging these methods, we demonstrate the ability to accurately model a variety of surface behaviors, including quasi-Chiral metasurfaces, and present the corresponding mathematical formulations. The framework is illustrated through the design of a wideband linear polarized anechoic metasurface, with simulations confirming the theoretical predictions. Implementing this method, we successfully realize a high-isolation RF MEMS switch, and the fabricated device shows excellent agreement with numerical simulations, achieving high isolation levels across multiple frequency bands. This method is highly versatile and can be applied to an array of complex metasurface applications.

The linear combination of local eCPNNs has been proposed as a simple, highly effective alternative to explain the strong electron correlations observed in extended systems. This method leverages local eCPNNs, which are trained to reproduce potential functions that capture the spatial relationships among electrons within atoms or molecules, providing a clear physical insight into the electron correlation mechanism. By comparing this approach to the traditional methods of band theory, our research demonstrates that the linear combination of local eCPNNs accurately captures the essential features of Fermi surface morphology, including the locations of critical points, shape, and size, consistent with the results obtained from the standard DFT calculations, while also showcasing the ability to predict material-specific correlations in potential functions. Furthermore, our work shows that the linear combination of local eCPNNs can be employed to analyze the correlations underlying the superconducting mechanism in the HfCuO$_2$ family by focusing on prototypical Ba$_{x}$Hf$_{1-x}$CuO$_2$. With this approach, we are able to identify the electron groups that contribute to superconductivity and demonstrate that the variety of materials properties observed within this series can be explained by a simple rotational symmetry breaking scenario. Our study provides a strong foundation for utilizing the linear combination of local eCPNNs in the comprehensive investigation of the electron correlation underlying superconductivity in the HfCuO$_2$ family and other complex materials systems. With further advancements in computational power and the development of more accurate eCPNN models, we can fully unlock the potential of this approach to explain the strong electron correlations observed in extended systems. We demonstrate how wide-field photometry can be utilized to determine vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) without relying on absolute calibration, drawing from the experiences of the CAWEE and ATOZ missions. VAOD is crucial for angular spectral broadening correction in long-path spectroscopy, among other applications. To calculate VAOD, we use the difference in twilight observations taken with different telescopes, leveraging the established approach of comparing sun scans with different angular separations as set by the width of the field of view. The accuracy of our method is validated through comparisons with established VAZ datasets, including both in situ and remotely sensed measurements. Furthermore, we incorporate VAOD retrievals into the angular spectral broadening correction algorithm and apply this to estimate CO$_2$ concentrations in the atmosphere during twilight observations. We also assess the effectiveness of VAOD retrievals with daily repeat cycles over the Equator using the GEMS satellite scenario, which incorporates VAOD-driven correction for a 10 d period during the dry season over Amazonas, Brazil, utilizing data from SCIA (now called ATOM) and showing an improvement of 1.5 $\mathrm{ppm}$ in CO$_2$ accuracy. This suggests that VAOD-based correction for angular spectral broadening can be an effective approach for improving CO$_2$ retrievals over tropical rainforest regions. However, it also indicates that further research is needed to ensure the method's robustness for daily repeat cycles over these areas. Finally, we examine the sensitivity of VAOD retrievals to different scalar versions of the Rayleigh optical thickness, highlighting the importance of accurate optical thickness determination for valid VAOD calculations. We also explore the possibility of VAOD applications beyond angular spectral broadening correction, citing potential uses in research related to cloud properties, optical thickness, and aerosol dynamics. Ultimately, we propose that the techniques outlined in this study could be adapted for other satellites, such as SCISAT and SBP, and suggest future VAOD retrieval validation be carried out in conjunction with in situ measurements collected during airborne missions like ATOZ and CAWEE. We propose a novel approach called Projection Clustering (PC) for 3D object pose estimation, which combats the issues of maximum likelihood (ML) estimators by dividing projections into sub-groups. By minimizing the sum of distances within each group, we redefine the pose estimation problem as an energy minimization task. A robust PC algorithm is developed by sequentially applying soft-deterministic grouping updates to projected images. Experimentation shows that our method outperforms multiple baseline algorithms and approaches the accuracy of global optimization methods on various 3D object datasets, including the benchmark KITTI dataset. Additionally, PC demonstrates the ability to handle multiple object poses in a scene. As the method's key innovation, projection clustering enables us to derive robust pose estimates through the minimization of energy functions in an efficient manner. This leads to several key advantages, including the capability to handle challenging real-world scenes as shown in Scene-Pose Dataset, a newly introduced dataset. We have developed a novel extension of the Graphical Lasso algorithm, called GLSC, by incorporating latent variables to expand the Sparsity Graphical Lasso framework. By adding a norm penalty to the second block of its parameters, the GLSC model represents the underlying structure of the latent variables as a directed acyclic graph. The GLSC algorithm achieves optimal score estimates through an iterative procedure involving Generalized Least Squares and delivers a guaranteed minimum of one sample per degree of freedom. The efficacy of the proposed method is validated through simulations and a real-world application, with results showing that GLSC outperforms the standard Graphical Lasso algorithm when modeling multiple structures. The implementation of the algorithm is made available online. The inclusion of latent variables in the GLSC model enhances the Lasso's structural discovery capabilities, demonstrating that a limited number of additional parameters can define a complete directed graph. The proposed method provides a framework for evaluating the consistency of structure estimation, with conditions relying on the Lasso's estimability and defined signal-to-noise ratios. The study's findings can be applied to various multiple-graphs scenarios, such as source detection, structure estimation, and graph segmentation. This study investigates how various numerical techniques influence the accuracy and computational speed of simulations for the alanine dipeptide, a crucial proxy for assessing methods in theoretical chemistry and pharmacology. We examine multiple methods, including ab initio integrators with high precision and learning-based algorithms with limited training, that demonstrate both high accuracy and fast computation times. Our analysis utilizes multiple metrics to evaluate these methods, considering both their average performance and variability across different starting conditions and situations. We also analyze the trade-offs between the time devoted to training and subsequent simulations, as well as the effects of using these methods for different time steps. Our research finds that the methods that exhibit the fastest computation times typically produce results with the highest accuracy, although some methods are remarkably close in terms of accuracy. Notably, one of the ab initio methods shows accuracy comparable to the most effective learning-based algorithms despite being significantly faster. Our analysis suggests that while ab initio methods generally require fewer steps for optimal results, learning-based algorithms can achieve similar accuracy with substantially fewer steps, leading to significant reductions in computational costs. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the value of comparing methods on a systematic basis, providing a framework for evaluating numerical methods on complex biomolecular systems like the alanine dipeptide. This framework enables the selection of the most appropriate method for specific use cases, considering factors like desired precision, computational resources, and the requirements of downstream applications. Our study includes an online database featuring results from an extensive set of simulations, offering a comprehensive basis for evaluating numerical methods on the alanine dipeptide through interactive data visualizations. This database will continue to be expanded to encompass additional systems and more advanced learning-based algorithms. The research presented here has been conducted in accordance with the ab initio guidelines established by the research community. The software used for the simulations and further research can be accessed through an open-source repository that includes detailed documentation and is compatible with a range of numerical integration methods. The findings from this study have significant implications for the development and evaluation of numerical methods for complex biomolecular systems, facilitating collaboration and the advancement of ab initio research. This research contributes to the study of multi-layer networks, focusing on the concept of node importance. A novel approach is introduced, in which the importance of a node in one layer affects its importance in another layer, subject to certain inter-layer constraints. We develop a robust learning guarantee for the Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, which involves incorporating a robust filter into the policy gradient method. Specifically, we demonstrate that FPG provides an efficient solution to minimizing an objective function that is affected by contaminated data. This paper introduces a new attention-based model called Dilated Dense Attention Unet, which achieves high accuracy in esophageal tumor segmentation. By combining the advantages of complex network architectures such as Unet and Attention Unet, DDAUnet uses dense attention blocks with diluted dilated convolutions to focus on crucial image features and regions. However, using attention blocks alone can lead to image noise suppression, so DDAUnet incorporates global and local attention blocks to balance detailed tumor features and eliminate noise. Compared to other popular models like Unet and Attention Unet, DDAUnet shows comparable or better performance on public benchmark datasets in the Kaggle EsophAge Challenge, with the benefit of using significantly fewer parameters. DDAUnet also successfully reduces the coefficient of variance in demonstration cases, proving its ability to generalize and produce consistent results. Real-time formation evaluation is a crucial process in oil and gas exploration and production, its speed and accuracy directly impacting operational decisions.  Due to constantly changing well conditions and the necessity to continuously update formation data from downlink phases, development departments face significant challenges determining the best approach for real-time formation estimation.  Our research addresses this issue by introducing a new method, LM-EnRML, derived from the exponential natural gradient method with memory for least-squares minimization.  This algorithm significantly outperforms existing methods, including the natural gradient method with memory for LS problems, and demonstrates even better performance compared to other popular formation evaluation methods, such as the iterative weighted least squares technique, SURF and FLAS.  By leveraging the memory of past data and utilizing the natural gradient direction, LM-EnRML enhances accuracy while minimizing the impact of noisy data, resulting in more precise formation evaluations.  We have developed a high-performance, parallelizable numerical approach for LM-EnRML, taking full advantage of computer processing capabilities to provide real-time results.  Successful field applications, backed by numerical simulations, validate the algorithm's superiority and efficiency.  This new method is now an integral part of the Halliburton's Formation Evaluation service in the company's intelligent wells division.  As a result, customers can enhance precision and speed of formation evaluation, ultimately leading to more informed operational decisions.  We intend for LM-EnRML to contribute to the advancement of research in real-time applications and make data optimization more efficient in general.  We have made the code for this algorithm available on open-source platforms, hoping it will benefit other scientists working on similar problems.  We plan to build on this success by continuing to develop and integrate this algorithm into other Halliburton applications. This study undertakes a theoretical examination of the named entity recognition task across various information access levels, from individual text entries to an entire corpus. Our analysis demonstrates how the incorporation of mid-level information, such as a collection of documents, influences the performance of NER models and addresses the long-standing question of whether NER can be learned from scratch across the entire corpus. By leveraging the distinction between local and global entity recognition, we propose a proposed model, the Co-NE model, which integrates corpus-level information to enhance the accuracy of NER. Experimental results on our designed NER tasks demonstrate the advantages of using corpus-level information. Additionally, our work validates previous observations indicating a significant gap in performance between zero-shot and finetuned models during regular NER tasks and explores various factors influencing the Co-NE model's effectiveness. Our code and data have been made publicly available for replication purposes.

The surge in AI-based image description tools raises concerns about their accessibility for visually impaired individuals who heavily rely on visual information and human-generated descriptions. Existing guidelines for describing images to the visually impaired date back over a decade and require update. We argue that simplified, flexible guidelines are necessary to facilitate the development of effective, efficient, and user-friendly image description tools. Through a large-scale survey of 2000 participants, we investigated users' current practices for searching visual content and their preferences for image descriptions. Analyzing users' response to a set of statement based on these findings, we identified associations with factors like age, searching frequency, and accessibility awareness. Our findings reveal intriguing patterns that may seem counter-intuitive at first glance. For example, despite frequent searching for visual content, middle-aged participants tended to opt for text-based search over video or image search. Furthermore, individuals with higher accessibility awareness preferred image descriptions, but surprisingly, so did those with lower accessibility awareness. Additionally, participants' description preferences correlated with their searching frequency rather than how they search for visual content. Lastly, surprising correlations emerged between users' description preferences and their demographic variables. We propose potential explanations for these findings and discuss their implications for designing image description tools, ultimately positioning them within the broader context of visual content search. Our research converges with efforts to develop more effective, user-centered tools that incorporate machine learning, and could serve as a foundation for further related studies. We make our survey and resulting data set available for the benefit of the research community. It comprises 2000 annotated data points from visually impaired individuals, offering a window into their visual content searching habits and image description preferences. It's our hope that this initiative will contribute to the development of more accessible and practical image description tools, ultimately enriching the user experience for this significant, often underserved user group. Our results also indicate that including exchange and correlation has a more substantial impact on spin-orbit coupling than expected, resulting in a shift of up to 0.15 eV in the plasmon energy in taunton liquids. This shift is proportional to the magnitude of spin-orbit coupling within these systems. The phenomenon of people sorting into like-minded online communities has significant consequences for the spread of misinformation. A notable effect of social media segregation is the reduced exposure to opposing views, which increases the likelihood of believing false information. This study examines how the big sort phenomenon affects the online spread of misinformation among users in geographically segregated areas using Twitter data from the 2016 US presidential election. It reveals that users who are geographically isolated tend to follow accounts that post false information and have limited access to accounts that post opposing views. This leads to an increase in the likelihood of users believing false information due to their decreased exposure to opposing views. It is also found that users in isolated areas have limited access to accounts that have previously been flagged for posting false information, which further contributes to the increased likelihood of believing false information. This research highlights the negative consequences of social media segregation on the spread of misinformation and suggests strategies to mitigate this issue. It also contributes to the existing literature on the effects of sorting phenomena on the spread of misinformation. This vision is closely tied to creating artificial neural networks that can learn and operate with minimal computational requirements and data inputs. By integrating logical rules into neural networks, operations that are not necessary can be eliminated during execution, reducing overall complexity. Moreover, incorporating external knowledge into the network enables it to process uncertain inputs more effectively. In this paper, a new framework that integrates logic rules and allows for efficient neural network decomposition is presented, along with an update rule that facilitates low-complexity neural network training using the least squares method. This approach is applied to an external memory attention mechanism model, leading to enhanced performance in low-resource settings and the ability to handle uncertain inputs. Experimental results show that this method achieves better outcomes than conventional attention models in tasks with limited data availability. Additionally, due to its low computational demands, this algorithm operates effectively on devices with restricted memory capacity. For instance, it successfully completes a 20K connection update batch without encountering issues, in contrast to conventional neural networks that often struggle with tens of thousands of connections. The proposed method also demonstrates a capacity to process uncertain inputs and display more prudent behavior during decisions. This is exemplified by its performance in a simple reward-based action selection task and the intelligent battery management system for electrical vehicles. With its efficient design, easy training, and innovative attention mechanism, this framework has tremendous potential to contribute to the development of neural networks for embedded mobile systems. We investigate the complex social task of teaching, focusing on its fundamental component: the exchange of product knowledge through speech. Divergent factors like demonstration type, audio instructions, subtasks, and errors significantly impact the conceptual content of the speech exchanged during the teaching process. Despite the richness and depth of this interaction, existing research has been limited to analyzing the structural aspects of the speech exchange system and neglecting its semantic aspects. In contrast, we introduce a method for semi-automatically identifying the conceptual content of the speech exchanged during the teaching process and apply it to study the variations of the conceptual content of the speech exchanged during the Amazon Mechanical Turk teaching process. Our results reveal significant differences in the conceptual content of the speech exchanged during the demonstration, instruction, subtask, and error phases, as well as variations in the conceptual content of the speech exchanged during the instruction and subtask phases. Additionally, we find that the conceptual content of the speech exchanged during the demonstration phase is distinct from that of the instruction phase. Furthermore, we find that users' previous responses influence the conceptual content of the speech exchanged during the subtask phase. In terms of the overall structure of the speech exchanged during the demonstration and instruction phases, we find evidence supporting the linear ordering of prototypical speech acts and the incorporation of the speech exchanged during the subtask and error phases into existing hierarchies. Our analysis of the conceptual content of the speech exchanged during the demonstration and instruction phases confirms the predicted distinctness of the two categories. However, only about 65% of the speech exchanged during the demonstration phase conveys new conceptual content as compared to the instruction phase, indicating significant overlap between the two. Moreover, error incidents primarily result in the exchange of new conceptual content, leading to an expansion of the existing conceptual knowledge. In contrast, subtask incidents mainly result in the repetition of existing conceptual content, confirming the linear ordering of prototypical speech acts and the incorporation of the speech exchanged during the subtask and error phases into existing hierarchies. Researchers have long recognized the connection between Euler-Arnold equations and the Fokker-Planck type equations with confinement. These equations play a crucial role in quantum field theory when determining instantons, providing a precise measure of energy barriers. Recently, novel methods for solving Euler-Arnold equations have emerged, enabling solutions for a range of manifolds, including Grassmannians and Stiefel manifolds. Building upon this progress, we apply these results to tackle complex, multi-Instanton problems by gradually subdividing the optimization task into more manageable components. Through this approach, we develop a quantum field theory Monte Carlo algorithm, capable of efficiently exploring the instanton landscape. In our studies, we investigate the renormalization group behavior within the pure Yang-Mills theory and observe results that exhibit consistent accuracy when compared to established data. Our innovative approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of Euler-Arnold equations but also opens up avenues for further computational investigations. Furthermore, the divisibility of Euler-Arnold equations may have far-reaching implications for the study of quantum field theories that involve manifold-valued fields. In our research, we concentrate on Yang-Mills theories, however our methods are sufficiently general to be applicable across a broader spectrum of quantum field theories. Moreover, our algorithm may be adapted for computational investigations of other complex energy landscapes. Ultimately, our studies serve as a starting point for a more comprehensive investigation that aims to establish a direct connection between the geometry of instanton landscapes and the renormal group. This relationship holds significant implications for our comprehension of fundamental physics, particularly in the context of string theory's dual universes, where instanton landscapes may serve as a fundamental building block for modeling energy landscapes. Consequently, our research may contribute to a better understanding of the physics governing the renormal group in such scenarios. In our current study, we focus exclusively on Yang-Mills theories; nevertheless, our methods are sufficiently general to be applicable across a broader spectrum of quantum field theories that feature manifold-valued fields. Consequently, our innovative approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of Euler-Arnold equations but also opens up avenues for further computational investigations of complex energy landscapes. Conversational interfaces are increasingly popular and part of many automated systems, but creating robust testing frameworks for them is a complex task. Current testing tools often rely on automated scripts in isolation, without considering the underlying system architecture. In response, we introduce a new approach called HypoCheck, which utilizes a specialized checker to analyze the underlying code and guide the generation of more effective and efficient test cases. By integrating HypoCheck with a state-of-the-art generative model, we have achieved notable improvements in conversational dialog quality, achieving a 19% decrease in poor dialog interactions and a 15% increase in user satisfaction, according to our evaluations using both automated metrics and human assessors. Our study showcases the benefits of integrating program analysis with machine learning-based conversational systems and paves the way for addressing other challenges in this area. The design and implementation considerations underlying HypoCheck also provide valuable insights into designing high-performance conversational systems. All code and data generated by our research are now available for public access.

This paper introduces a cross-lingual memory retriever to enhance bilingual translation memory for low-resource language translation. By leveraging a high-resource language and a strong model, the retriever can extract relevant memories from the target language for low-resource languages. The cross-lingual memory retriever is trained on two tasks: using English as a bridge for Aramaic-to-English translation, and using French as a bridge for English-to-French translation. The results show the method improves translation quality significantly compared to traditional bilingual memory approaches, with the best model achieving an improvement of 1.5 in BLEU score for Aramaic-to-English translation and 1.8 for English-to-French translation, an 8.4% and 5.5% increase respectively. The code and data used in the research are available at this link https://github.com/ghossoun/cx-lm-retriever. The findings suggest combining a strong model of a high-resource language with a weak model of a low-resource language can effectively enhance the translation quality. The method also offers an efficient way to develop machine translation systems for low-resource languages with limited labeled data, requiring only unsupervised data from the target language, except for the case of translating into a language that also requires labeled data. The method also improves the translation quality when used with labeled data, but to a lesser extent. The method's performance can be further improved by using more powerful models and better encoding methods. The research presents several successful applications, including using a model trained on Arabic dialects to improve translation of standard Arabic, and using a model trained on Israeli text to improve translation of Egyptian Arabic. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated across a range of domains and languages, showing potential as a standard method for developing machine translation systems in low-resource settings. The method also offers an efficient way to combine multiple resources in a language, improving translation quality for domains with limited data by leveraging domains with abundant data. The method's potential is thought to stem from its ability to extract target language memories using a high-resource language as a bridge. Recent research suggested that certain large-scale cosmic structures, specifically low-variance circles and Hawking points, could be observable in the sky. However, these features would likely be masked by the inherent irregularities inherent in the cosmic microwave background, resulting from the effects of the universe's gravitational instability and gravitational waves. Notably, proposed models incorporating a four-dimensional Hawking radiation could explain the formation of these large-scale structures. Although the associated energy scales and time frames are highly variable, certain scenarios do share common characteristics. For instance, the majority of multiverse simulations predict a distinctive pattern - an isolated "dot" or ring-like structure. Furthermore, studies indicate that future generative models will be capable of accurately simulating the cosmic microwave background by incorporating a level of stability. Consequently, under such conditions, the features of Hawking points would become indistinguishable from natural variations in the cosmic microwave background. However, certain models involving a Hawking radiation in five-dimensional spaces may still be testable by analyzing local fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background, offering a possible means of verifying the theory of Hawking radiation. A well-established challenge in developing automated analysis solutions for MRI data is ensuring that the models don't solely rely on the characteristics of the training dataset. We investigated how the presence of scans from other populations affects model performance on unseen MRI data, specifically knee MRIs, by introducing a small amount of diverse scans during training. We used public datasets and those collected in-house for our research. We discovered that when we added a limited number of diverse scans (around 100) to the training dataset, which significantly differed (various knee pathologies, ages 18-75, multiple centers), there was a notable decrease in the model's accuracy. However, when we introduced a more substantial amount of diverse scans (around 1500) with a wider age range (ages 19-88), there was only a minimal decrease in accuracy with the current dataset but further increases in diversity didn't seem to affect the model's performance in our experiments. We analyzed the models' performance with and without the diverse scans using a theoretical approach that takes into account noise and variability. We found that by introducing an appropriate regularization, such as noise and extra Scans, can lead to a minimal decrease in accuracy. This can be understood through the lens of Generalized Cross Validation. We also found that the optimal weight for the regularization term is not always the best indicator of the models' performance on unseen data. Instead, the effective number of degrees of freedom, which is highly influenced by the diversity, can serve as a better predictor. Our research provides valuable insights into designing robust models that can adapt to unseen data, essentially a model that can adapt to the concept of "average". We also found that the effective number of degrees of freedom is highly correlated with the diversity of the training dataset. This is measured by calculating the effective number of degrees of freedom for each scan individually and then taking the average and standard deviation across all training scans. We believe that our approach can be applied to a broad range of problems where the goal is to evaluate the performance of models on unseen data that significantly differs from the training dataset. A novel file system called NOVA-relaxed NVMM file system has been developed to optimize the use of Optane DC Persistent Memory Modules (PMMs) for persistent memory mapping (PMMs). This study evaluates the performance of this file system by conducting a range of experiments, including evaluations of various file system operations, database performance, web server throughput, and the relaxation of memory persistence models. Notably, our evaluations revealed that the original NOVA NVMM file system could lead to substantial performance degradation for applications with small, frequent persistent writes. To address this issue, we modified the file system to create the NOVA-relaxed NVMM file system, which significantly improves performance in such scenarios. Compared to the original NVMM file system, the relaxed version reduces average request handling time by 75ms, decreases tail latencies by 90%, and boosts write throughput up to 10 times. Moreover, the relaxed scheme boasts similar performance to the original no-fault-tolerant file system for large, infrequent persistent writes. Additionally, our evaluations demonstrate that the NOVA-relaxed NVMM file system supports various applications, including MySQL, PostgreSQL, and LiteCores, with only minor reductions in performance, typically around 10%. Furthermore, we found that the original and relaxed schemes exhibit similar benchmark results in terms of throughput, latency, and tail latencies for various workloads, including TPCC, YCSB, and Memcached. To facilitate replication and verification, the source code, benchmarks, and data associated with this study have been made available online. This research has been conducted using a workload manager called NWManager, a modular, extensible manager built using lightweight, threadless components to provide low-latency storage services. Lastly, our findings indicate that the NOVA-relaxed NVMM file system can deliver substantial performance improvements for applications with small, persistent writes, and it is suitable for a range of use cases, including those mentioned above. This study provides valuable insights into the performance characteristics of NOVA-relaxed NVMM file systems and identifies several directions for further research and optimization. Next, a range of pre-defined shapes are used to identify potential tumor locations through subtraction and erosion processes. A secondary evaluation is performed on the identified areas to eliminate any noise and false detections. The viable tumor shapes are ranked according to their size and shape complexity, and the top candidate is selected for validation against actual tumor measurements. A comparative analysis is conducted among traditional detection methods, including template matching and the use of artificial intelligence. The proposed method is implemented using C++ and ITK-SNAP software, and is accessible online at https://bitbucket.org/azayed/brain-tumor-detection. Researchers using radial velocity surveyors often employ a method to randomize the selection of lines from pre-computed lists to alleviate RV jitter. This technique involves picking lines at random from a computed list to minimize the impact of radial velocity jitter. This approach to line selection has been successful, and our findings confirm it induces less radial velocity jitter compared to a more straightforward method of choice based on spectral parameters. Furthermore, we discovered that a randomized strategy has a lower RV jitter level compared to another method of choice, which involves picking lines that are structurally similar to the target and has a lower RV amplitude. This method of line selection by evaluation has a higher RV jitter level because it requires generating multiple combinations of lines during the target observation. Consequently, we propose that future high-resolution high-stability RV surveyors be equipped with the capability to generate random line selections from pre-computed lists to minimize RV jitter during actual observations. Additionally, we suggest developing software to generate random selections, minimize the memory requirements for line lists, and provide users with an intuitive interface for configuring line selection parameters. This approach allows for greater scientific flexibility and better data quality. As an illustration, we show the results of randomizing line lists for a specific K-dwarf star. The success of modern recommenders relies heavily on entity representations, which are usually learned through embedding methods with low dimensional structures. However these methods typically focus on preserving the similarity or dissimilarity of adjacent entities in a graph, without considering the underlying topology. As a result, entities with similar topology but no direct connection in the graph may have poor recommendations due to limited relevance. To address this issue, we propose EntityGraphMix, a novel method that allows entities to maintain their topological structure while being learned from embedding dynamics during random walks. EntityGraphMix combines the insights gained from dynamic representations and the structural information of the graph to produce high-quality entity representations. By leveraging the diversity of random walk paths, EntityGraphMix achieves more diverse dynamic representations, which enhances the robustness of the recommended results. Experimental results on three real-world datasets demonstrate EntityGraphMix's capability to produce entiti representations with both high quality and diversity, leading to superior recommendation performance. Notably, EntityGraphMix outperforms state-of-the-art methods by achieving a significant 12% improvement in diversity and 5% improvement in quality, according to our experiments. Our code is available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/EntityGraphMix. This research introduces a novel financial text embedding model called Tushre, which leverages a dictionary-based approach to generate representations that accurately capture the meanings of words in the financial sector. Unlike conventional embedding techniques, existing methods often confuse opposites like "profit" and "loss" as similar meanings. This research addresses this challenge by recognizing that antonyms should not be considered synonyms. Furthermore, the proposed model distinguishes between the frequency of opposites and the intensity of antonyms, which is essential in financial contexts where the frequent occurrence of opposites can indicate a balanced state and the intense presence of an antonym can indicate a highly unstable condition. We evaluate Tushre by assessing its ability to preserve the intensity and frequency of antonyms and synonyms in financial texts and demonstrate its superiority over alternative embedding models. Additionally, we show that Tushre can be an effective tool for sentiment analysis by incorporating an artificial neural network classifier into the model. The results of our analysis reveal that Tushre outperforms existing financial text embedding models and achieves accurate classifications in various financial text datasets. The source code for Tushre is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/abhishekmitra420/Tushre. The financial text datasets employed in this research can be obtained from https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/Tushre_Datasets. The code for the artificial neural network classifier is hosted at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/Tushre_Cross_Entropy. The dictionary-based approach utilized in Tushre is based on the NSE dictionary comprising 13,509 unique words. The model's representations and results are openly accessible at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/Tushre_Embeddings. The current iteration of Tushre processes embeddings at a rate of approximately 10 GB per hour using a single GPU. This paper classifies wideband waveforming techniques into two categories and provides mathematical formulations for minimizing and maximizing fair-throughput and sum-throughput respectively. Fair-throughput refers to the minimum achievable rate of poor users, while sum-throughput is the total achievable rate across all users. We develop optimality conditions for fair-throughput and sum-throughput and propose a sub-optimal closed-loop solution for fair-throughput via waterfilling. For sum-throughput, we propose a sub-optimal open-loop solution using combinatorial algorithms. We apply our framework to a cognitive radio network and a SWIPT network, solving for fair-throughput and sum-throughput in these scenarios. Simulations show our waveforming strategies outperform traditional power allocation methods. Additionally, increasing the number of antennas at the transmitter or cognitive users' information generation rates can significantly boost sum-throughput but has a less pronounced impact on fair-throughput. Furthermore, our closed-loop fair-throughput solution can adapt quickly to changing environmental conditions. Lastly, our results demonstrate the feasibility of our solutions with modern digital signal processing capabilities. We employ a hybrid approach using a low-dimensional model and an artificial viscosity method to simulate the Rayleigh--Bénard instability in an enclosed, viscous fluid under intense temperature differences. Despite being a highly complex phenomenon, the Rayleigh--Bénard instability has only a few degrees of freedom in motion. The hybrid approach leverages the low-dimensional model's ability to capture the underlying dynamics and the artificial viscosity method's ability to eliminate the need for resolving the entire turbulence spectrum. By combining these approaches, we aim to focus on the primary oscillatory modes occurring within the system by reducing the degrees of freedom and introducing a non-uniform viscosity that counteracts turbulence, thus allowing us to simulate the interaction of unstable modes at different frequencies. This methodology is applied to a two-dimensional square box and yields detailed visualizations and frequency spectra, revealing the development of the Rayleigh--Bénard instability and the resulting Taylor--Proudman flow. Our method also generates unusual patterns of circulation at the boundary layers and the discovery of the primary oscillatory frequency decreasing with increasing Marangoni number. This is further confirmed by our results which show the primary frequency separating from the high-frequency turbulence by our method. The detection of this frequency separation offers a possible explanation for the existence of the intermediate temperature regime in the Marangoni--Rayleigh--Bénard instability. This study analyzes how the correlated Rayleigh fading and phase shifts of reflecting coefficients impact the average data transfer rate of a wireless communication system, also considering the impact of co-polar and cross-polar fading factors. Initially, we establish mathematical relationships between the defined variables through their respective probability distribution functions and correlations. Subsequently, we derive and model the average data transfer rate as a function of these variables and their products, which represent the system's performance from both an absolute and relative perspective. We further develop an alternative model for the average data transfer rate in terms of the product of two mathematical functions, one related to the fading distribution and the other to the phase shift, and apply this model to analyze the impact of various system and environmental factors. Finally, we validate our model through simulations and provide relative sensitivity analyses to establish their practical utility.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a novel code utilizing the Tree-PM method that generates gravitational potentials for N-body simulations. MG-GLAM is an enhancement of the GLAM code, which used an octree-based multigrid technique, though it suffered from high computational costs. By integrating the tree-PM method, MG-GLAM leverages the strengths of both approaches - the octree's efficient force calculation and the high accuracy of its potential - while reducing total computational time by approximately tenfold during a key test scenario. This significant improvement, achieved through the integration of highly parallelizable components, makes MG-GLAM an exceptionally fast code. Additionally, MG-GLAM maintains the simplicity and ease of use that characterized its predecessor. As such, it represents an extremely attractive option for researchers requiring accurate, high-resolution potential maps generated through N-body simulations. As part of the code's assessment, MG-GLAM was compared to both the original GLAM code and the widely used Gadget-2 code, yielding results that validate its performance and accuracy. A nonlocal gravity model is proposed, based on an altered constitutive relation that involves the double differential operator, which is equivalent to a first-order nonlocal theory. We demonstrate that this operator can be represented by a combination of first and second-order nonlocal theories. The new framework yields unique predictions for the nonlocal scale and its impact on existing phenomena, such as gravitational waves and the de Sitter solution. Additionally, it is shown that the proposed model relates to Herberth-Wheeler's work and results in a nonlocal gravity model of first-order. The new theory also differs from Finkelstein's nonlocal gravity model, especially in the context of the nonlocal scale's influence. We explore the nonlocal gravitational field equations in an isotropic flat universe and analyze the effectiveness of this model in explaining certain observational data sets. The model proves capable of reproducing the late-universe behavior seen in Type Ia supernovae and the cosmic microwave background, but falls short of mimicking the universe's evolution during its early stages. Nonetheless, it is evident that a multi-component universe may be a viable approach. The fundamental parameters of the model are determined through a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method and it is found that the nonlocal scale is on the order of $10^{16}$ meters. The model predicts a value of $4.4\times 10^{-3}$ for the Newtonian constant at the nonlocal scale, in addition to a cosmological constant-like behavior. The new theory presents an interesting perspective on the fundamental principles of gravity, offering a framework that could be experimentally tested through experiments focused on gravitational waves and gravity at the atomic scale. This, in turn, may lead to a deeper comprehension of the human's place within the universe. The number of known neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries in our Galaxy remains limited, which makes the exact population size highly uncertain. This study aims to fill this gap by utilizing all available information on these binaries. A key aspect of our analysis is the recognition that every low-mass X-ray binary that reaches the end of its active phase and sheds its disk can generate a millisecond radio pulsar. Therefore, we first determine the total population of radio pulsars with this characteristic properties by extrapolating the detection data, considering factors such as volume coverage, pulsar spin period and period derivative. Once the total population is calculated, we can derive the underlying population of low-mass X-ray binaries, which produces these pulsars. Our analysis yields a total population of 1.02 +/- 0.24 x 10^-3 galaxies with similar specific characteristics, and an intrinsic rate of formation of low-mass X-ray binaries of 8.9 x 10^-6 yr^-1 Galactic century^-1. However, we note that this figure may be affected by observational biases, given the limited number of detected binaries. Nevertheless, it serves as a useful starting point for further theoretical and observational studies of these fascinating objects. It also allows us to estimate the probability of discovering a low-mass X-ray binary with known millisecond radio pulsar properties in existing X-ray surveys, as well as the characteristics of future generation telescopes. Lastly, we identify several candidates to be monitored in the near future for possible pulsar activity, including the low-mass X-ray binaries V404 Cygni, 4U 1624-49 and XTE J1143-640. It is our hope that this study will contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between low-mass X-ray binaries and millisecond radio pulsars, and ultimately, the dynamics that govern their formation and evolution. We examine how multiple algebraic weights influence the geometric modularity of a non-algebraic weight at a prime, emphasizing the significance of Serre's conjecture and the geometric version of it. By analyzing algebraic weights and their relationship to non-algebraic weights, we establish conditions for geometric modularity of a weight in terms of the geometric modularity of multiple weights. This framework allows us to derive results for both weight-zero and non-zero weights. Specifically, we demonstrate that certain families of modular forms or Galois representations achieve geometric modularity, driven by the geometric modularity of algebraic weights in a range of situations. This includes instances where geometric modularity arises locally at all primes or a specific prime, and scenarios where it emerges for weights within a specific range or after applying base change. Alongside, we provide examples and applications related to Shimura varieties and Hida families. Ultimately, our study offers strategies for predicting the geometric modularity of non-algebraic weights, ultimately contributing to solving conjectures like the Geometric Serre Weight Conjecture. These strategies also enable us to solve a special case of the conjecture for weight zero at all primes or a specific prime, respectively. A combined numerical and analytical jet afterglow model has been developed, addressing criticisms of the traditional one-zone model. This improved model represents a circular jet with equal energy distribution across different particles' energies. It accounts for both ultra-relativistic and non-relativistic phases, using a first-order Boltzmann equation and Monte Carlo simulations. The model includes a broad spectral energy distribution, encompassing gamma-rays, X-rays, optical, and radio waves, utilizing a synthetic approach. It integrates an external radiation field interaction, treating adiabatic losses, and it has been compared to observational data from six events, resulting in satisfactory fittings. These comparisons demonstrate that the traditional one-zone model's limitations arise from its inability to accurately depict the jet's global characteristics rather than its relativistic nature. The new model offers a comprehensive alternative to traditional one-zone models, making it an improved tool for interpreting jet afterglow phenomena.

In graph theory, splitting vertices is a local transformation where a vertex is broken into two non-adjacent ones, connected to the original neighbors. This work explores the potential of combining this transformation with edge splitting (introducing a new edge between two existing vertices) to simplify drawing certain types of graphs. Focusing on planar drawings, we investigate the impact of these operations on bipartite and forest graphs. Our findings demonstrate that using vertex splitting alone can planarly draw any bipartite graph with k vertex splittings, any k-edge planar bipartite graph, and any forest graph with k edge splittings. However, we also show that a forest graph may require an exponential number of vertex splittings, even if edges can be added freely. In contrast, a recent study proved the ability to planarly draw any forest graph using vertex and edge splittings, although the proof lacks a quantitative bound on the number of vertex splittings. Building on that research, we establish a new upper limit for the number of vertex splittings required to draw any forest graph. This new threshold is significantly lower, at no more than 3 times the number of vertices in the graph, when considering both free and restricted vertex and edge splittings. Deep learning models often suffer from score calibration issues, which can be compounded by classification imbalance. We investigate how popular calibration methods affect the performance of Inception Score (IS) metrics, which assess the generative quality of synthetic data. The impact of these techniques is examined across three scenarios featuring significant class imbalance. The findings suggest that certain calibration methods significantly alter IS calculations in a way that mistakenly benefits generative models, ultimately failing to address the underlying issues. Alternatively, we propose an alternative IS implementation that takes the imbalance into account, yielding more accurate and reliable results. The proposed method proves capable of distinguishing between generative model quality and the impact of imbalance in IS calculations. Comprehensive experiments validate the proposed method's effectiveness and highlight the limitations of existing calibration techniques in the context of IS metrics. The code for the proposed method is available online.

Closed-loop feedback control techniques have been successfully integrated with bipedal robots to enhance their locomotion efficiency and stability. This study investigates how closed-loop feedback and external forces influence a bipedal robot's gait dynamics. We develop an analytical model to examine the impact of closed-loop feedback on the robot's double support phase, finding it to be sensitive to feedback and external forces. Furthermore, we establish that the robot's asymmetric gaits can be broken down into a symmetric base gait combined with an asymmetrical swing phase movement. We also present a second-order model to analyze the swing phase, revealing that its frequency can be adjusted through co-design of the double support and swing phases. We demonstrate the applicability of our findings to a humanoid robot, the Robin, by conducting experiments on him, with results showing a notable improvement in accuracy when using our model. Our study provides valuable insights into the design of bipedal robots, highlighting the importance of considering the interactions between closed-loop feedback, external forces, and the robot's dynamics to achieve optimal performance. We contribute our developed model to the community as a tool to analyze and optimize the gait of closed-loop bipedal robots. To achieve a higher level of accuracy in new physics searches at future colliders such as HL-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, ILC, CLIC, CEPC, and CPPC, refining existing theoretical precision methods is necessary. Despite the importance of weak-boson production, calculations for this process are already technically feasible; however, developing new approaches to simplify existing time-consuming calculations will still be necessary to meet the needs of these future colliders. To address this challenge, we have derived a new set of analytical formulas to calculate arbitrary combinations of unpolarized observables in electroweak vector-boson production, which can be applied to a wide range of colliders, including those with vector-boson scattering at 1 TeV to several TeV of energy, and also extend previous research that was limited to a maximum energy of around 1.8 TeV. These new formulas can be used to calculate unstable particle distributions, such as W and Z bosons, and also stable particle distributions, such as di-lepton and di-boson combinations, and can be combined with experimental resolution functions to account for instrumental effects. We have further developed a public code to support these new formulas and demonstrate its capabilities through a set of representative scenarios. This code can also be adapted to accommodate specific requirements of individual experiments at future colliders. By providing this code and its underlying theoretical framework, we aim to contribute to the development of precise theoretical predictions for weak-boson production in the context of the Standard Model and its extensions. This code can be accessed through our public repository at the provided link.

Furthermore, we show that learning certain attributes like gender and age is inherently inseparable from learning the target data in VertFL. Our results demonstrate that HardMax achieves stronger privacy guarantees than existing protocols, and we provide theoretical evidence that it can provide quantitative privacy protection against a wide range of attacks. By examining the properties of these features, this research demonstrates the advantages of PRFF over RFF in terms of both dimension reduction and predictive accuracy. Additionally, this work establishes guidelines for selecting the number of PRFF features, which can lead to more efficient kernel methods. This efficient approach to feature map design is demonstrated through its application to a support vector machine. This research focuses on examining the finite-element method for a specific variational damage model that incorporates oscillatory behavior and is applied to heterogeneous materials. A gradient-based model is utilized, defined by minimizing a functional that includes both bulk and surface components. The model is defined by the space $A(\bar{Q})$, where $\bar{Q}$ represents the reference configuration of a non-degenerate body $Q$. To account for the uncertainty caused by resolving resolution limits in numerical simulations, an oscillatory function is introduced and is assumed to be sufficiently smooth. Given this framework, we establish the existence of a strong solution and demonstrate that the proposed model produces unique strong solutions in both the time-dependent and stationary cases. Additionally, an energy estimate is derived to demonstrate the convergence of strong solutions to a steady state. To analyze the spatial variability of materials, we introduce the concept of fractional material homogenization. Through this approach, we derive homogenized formulations for both fixed and moving boundaries. The proposed approach overcomes the previous limitation of requiring material smoothness by utilizing the concept of oscillatory functions. This enables us to consider non-smooth materials while maintaining the integrity of energy estimates. The results are validated through numerical experiments implemented in the Dune framework using the Boa library. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through a convergence study of a typical problem. The associated code is publicly accessible online. The novel approach introduced in this research addresses the challenge of modeling gradient damage in heterogeneous materials, providing a more general and flexible framework.
