We establish the applicability of cdh descent and Milnor excision in this context and explore the related consequences of Quillen excision. Our findings enable us to derive the homotopy K-theoretic version of the cdh-Milnor excision theorem originally proved by Kahn and Lipshitz. We also develop a converse for a portion of this conclusion's results. Moreover, we demonstrate the equivalence of cdh descent and Milnor excision to Quillen excision with support in the category of finitely presented projective modules for various self-equivalences of the sphere spectrum. This investigation is further enriched by the introduction of cdh-Milnor excision for twisted conjugacy classes within the context of the Thomifification procedure. Here, we establish the compatibility of cdh-Milnor excision with the twisted conjugation action on homotopy K-theory, thereby extending our earlier findings to this more refined level of precision. This research is also presented alongside an exploration of Heegaard diagrams and their relationship to twisted conjugacy classes, enabling us to formulate and explore conjectures regarding cdh-Milnor excision's applicability in this context. Recent studies suggest that 1,2-pyridine diolefin (1,2-PDO) may serve as an efficient scaffold for activating methylarenes towards methylation. To gain insight into the mechanistic differences between 1,2-PDO and 1,3-PDO, the former was employed to methylate a selection of arenes. Interestingly, the facility of methylating arenes correlates with the ease of cyclohexadienyl cation formation, which is influenced by ring strain. This knowledge was used to design a series of arenes that preferentially stabilize primary cyclohexadienyl cations over the methyl cation. Surprisingly, these arenes were found to undergo efficient methylation, likely as a result of the directing effect of the adjacent nitrogen atom. This effect is thought to increase the energy of the methyl cation relative to the cyclohexadienyl cation, allowing the arenes to undergo methylation with high facility despite being ortho-disubstituted. In contrast, meta-disubstituted arenes that preferentially stabilize primary cyclohexadienyl cations over the methyl cation undergo methylation with high facility. However, ortho-disubstituted arenes that preferentially stabilize the methyl cation over the cyclohexadienyl cation are resistant to methylation. This work highlights the potential of 1,2-PDO to activate methylarenes towards methylation and demonstrates the importance of distinguishing between the directing effects of nitrogen and methyl groups. Additionally, a proposed mechanism for the methylation of arenes employs a [2+2] cyclohexadienyl methyl cation intermediate. The ability to selectively activate methylarenes towards methylation may be realized through the design of more sophisticated, higher-order pdolefins that can differentiate between nitrogen and methyl substituents. This could enable the methylation of arenes that cannot be efficiently methylated under present conditions. Finally, a proposed strategy for designing such molecules is outlined. This strategy involves identifying suitable candidates and assessing their ability to activate methylarenes towards methylation using computational modeling. A proposed protocol for conducting these computations efficiently is also outlined. This protocol leverages a previously developed tool, DDEC6-Shanghai, to compute molecular properties that correlate with experimental reactivity trends. The ability to distinguish between the directing effects of nitrogen and methyl groups using this approach has not been previously reported. This work has implications for the design of molecules that can selectively activate and modify specific functional groups

Measuring the fidelity between two global states is a fundamental task that has been applied to various quantization methods, including tensor networks and quantum circuits. While estimating the fidelity is computationally intensive for global states, we demonstrate that, for equilibrated states from quantum circuits, a different approach yields efficient results. Firstly, we convert the tensor network description to a circuit-like format using a two-qubit unitary matrix transformation method. Secondly, we calculate the fidelity between two states by measuring the overlap between their associated circuits. This measurable fidelity is itself expressible through a global operator that is circuit-born and efficiently computable. Consequently, measuring the fidelity between two equilibrated states from quantum circuits reduces to estimating the equilibrated state itself, which can be accomplished with $O(2^n)$ efficiency for an $n$-qubit system. This method generalizes previous analyses and enhances the understanding of quantum circuits as a type of tensor network. Additionally, it facilitates the estimation of fidelity between any two states from quantum circuits with repeated applications of the same unitary matrix and corresponding measurements. A recent discovery made by Chen, Li, and Yang suggests that certain conserved current block operators in two-dimensional conformal field theory can be represented as AdS$_3$ geodesic operators. However, when these operators are expressed in terms of AdS$_2$ geodesic operators, their representations change to non-conserving blocks. We plan to extend the finding by identifying additional conserved current blocks and examining their AdS$_2$ and AdS$_3$ operator equivalents in both the symmetric and asymmetric cases. Moreover, we demonstrate the application of this duality in determining the four-point function of stress tensors in minimal models with conserved currents, and verify the results against existing literature. Our study utilizes the AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ duality to illustrate a method for obtaining the AdS$_3$ four-point function for conformal graviton and gravamagnet in the context of the 2+1 dimensional Brown-Duval gravity. This approach allows us to accurately determine the bulk dimension of the AdS$_3$ operator corresponding to the stress tensors, which is parameterized in terms of the spin and conformal weight. We find that for spin-two gravitons, the bulk dimension is $\frac{d}{2} = 1$, and for spin-one gravamagnets, the bulk dimension is $\frac{d}{2} = 1 + \frac{\ell}{\pi}$, where $\ell$ is the conformal weight, which provides a novel interpretation of the positive energy theorem in gravity with a negative cosmological constant. We also derive the AdS$_3$ operator corresponding to general conserved currents and verify the proposed expression against existing literature in the context of the $sl(2)$ symmetry. Lastly, we examine the cross-channel contribution and the AdS$_3$ operator factorization in the context of the graviton four-point function, which validates the proposed expression. Our study offers further evidence for the AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ duality and provides a useful method for deriving the AdS$_3$ four-point function directly from the CFT$_2$ perspective. This approach may also be applied to derive the AdS$_3$ five-point function, which is of great interest in the context of the BTZ black hole. We assess the effectiveness of various neural network approaches in identifying galaxy clusters through lensing analysis by comparing them to traditional methods. This marks a significant step towards maximizing the scientific potential of future weak-lensing cluster studies.

Researchers have identified a long-standing issue with cosmological simulations, specifically regarding their halo mass predictions, which exhibit an unanticipated dependence on the density of the initial conditions. This effect, initially noticed in the $N$-body simulation of a flat low-density universe with a 0.3 redshift, has since been confirmed in various scenarios, including models of a 0.7 universe and those featuring dark energy. Studies have demonstrated that creating a realistic distribution of halos requires not only the proper amplitude of initial scalar perturbations but also a specific level of primordial power, which is directly proportional to the square of the universe's density parameter. This finding implies that a simple density-only model is insufficient for accurately predicting the mass of halos in a universe with a different density parameter than that of our local universe. However, it appears that when the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations is adjusted proportionally to the change in the universe's density parameter, the desired halo mass distribution is replicated. Nevertheless, when the amplitude of primordial power is adjusted in this manner, the effect on the halo mass spectrum becomes significant, resulting in an excessive number of low-mass halos and a shortage of intermediate-mass halos. Consequently, when constructing large-scale structure models based on cosmological simulations, it is necessary to incorporate a more intricate relationship between the universe's density parameter and the halo mass spectrum, one that goes beyond a simple density-only model. Upcoming high-resolution simulations will allow for a comprehensive examination of the halo mass spectrum in a wide range of density parameter amplitudes, and in the meantime, a simple theoretical model is proposed to explain the observed dependence of the halo mass spectrum on the density parameter of the universe. This model is contingent on the structure of primordial fluctuations and the halo mass spectrum formed as a result of gravitational evolution, and it effectively captures the interplay between the merger history of halos and the universe's density parameter. As a result of this model, a specific relationship between the amplitude of primordial power and the density parameter of the universe is proposed, featuring a distinct "plateau" at high densities, and it is further suggested that this model may be applicable to a broader range of cosmological scenarios. The detection of gravitational waves from the merger of neutron stars or black holes is significantly enriched by simultaneous electromagnetic radiation observations. To fully leverage the potential of multi-messenger astronomy, it's essential to accurately associate electromagnetic counterparts with gravitational waves. As the LIGO/VIRGO network and electromagnetic telescopes will soon be joined by third-generation gravitational wave detectors and more sensitive telescopes, the field will transform in the coming decades. However, the challenge of identifying counterparts in a data-rich future poses a significant problem. In this paper, a new method for associating electromagnetic radiation with gravitational waves is introduced. This approach uses a machine learning algorithm that effectively utilizes the relevant characteristics of electromagnetic radiation and its temporal and spectral characteristics. The new method is designed to outperform existing association techniques even when the signal-to-noise ratio is low. Two methods for incorporating the characteristics of electromagnetic radiation's temporal and spectral properties into the algorithm are also proposed. The performance of these methods is evaluated under various future detection scenarios. As a result, this research provides an innovative solution to an important problem in multi-messenger astronomy and offers relevant expertise that can be adapted to address other challenges in gravitational wave research. This expertise includes best practices for processing gravitational wave signals and the application of machine learning to strain data. Furthermore, this work includes several recommendations for enhancing the detection of electromagnetic radiation counterparts in future low-signal-to-noise-ratio scenarios. This will become increasingly relevant as the sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors continues to improve and a wider range of electromagnetic counterparts is detected. This research is timely, given the significant discoveries already made in this field, such as GW170817, and is expected to contribute positively to the further breakthroughs expected in the field of multi-messenger astronomy. Researchers propose that massive young stars may maintain their extreme rotation rates through the impact of migrating objects in their surrounding discs. Despite initial studies indicating this theory might be plausible, its viability remains largely untested. To further investigate, a newly developed numerical model simulates the influence of migrating objects on inner discs, revealing how they can stabilize and alter the dynamics near their edges. Notably, the simulated area exhibits characteristic patterns of activity seen in EUV and X-ray spectra. The model also successfully replicates the observed patterns of activity in stars similar to VX Sagittarii and the recent findings surrounding the PDS 66 system. However, attempting to apply the model to stars as massive as VX Sagittarii reveals that it fails to replicate the stars' extremely high rotation rates. A possible explanation for this failure is the presence of outer discs in these stars, which could be contributing to their rapid spin down. We introduce the concept of half-positional winning conditions as a more flexible alternative to positional winning conditions, allowing for more complex strategies to be defined using the union of prefix-independent properties. Positional conditions can be formulated using a limited set of formulas that only incorporate symmetry operations, whereas half-positional conditions encompass all possibilities. We demonstrate that the union of multiple half-positional conditions, each independent of the prefix, can still yield a non-half-positional winning condition. Building upon this concept, we explore the intersection of half-positional conditions and the intersection of finite automata in games played on finite graphs. Our research reveals that the union of two independent half-positional conditions results in a non-half-positional condition, whereas the intersection of all half-positional conditions is equivalent to the intersection of all positional conditions. We also establish that the game of alternating reachability half-positional conditions on finite graphs is NP-complete. Moreover, we examine games defined by multiple half-positional conditions that involve symmetry operations and demonstrate that determining whether such games have winning conditions for either player is computationally NP-complete. Additionally, we present an algorithm analyzing game complexity for a specific class of anti-finite automata games. Our research paves the way for further exploration into the properties of half-positional conditions and their applications in analyzing parity conditions and other multi-player games. Our methodology involves the use of simplified formulations for half-positional conditions and the union of prefix-independent conditions to provide more intuitive understanding of these concepts. Our research includes the development of methods for defining half-positional conditions and the union of prefix-independent conditions through finite automata, enabling us to establish the computational complexity of various multi-player games. Our findings open up new directions for studying complex games and strategies in mathematical logic and computer science. Our research is also relevant to the study of game theory and algebraic decision properties in finite graphs. The calculus of constructions, introduced by Girard, has significantly impacted the development of modern programming languages and type theory. Its innovations, such as constructing terms to prove judgments, have been adopted by various languages and theories. This project's website and reference manual detail the definition of a structured version of the calculus, incorporating features from contemporary programming and type theories, such as dependent patterns, functions with multiple arguments, and a structured product operator. Building on previous work by Urban et al., the project's implementation utilizes the Coq proof assistant to demonstrate the calculus' capabilities and showcase its utility as a tool for formalizing programming languages and type theories within the Coq ecosystem. By integrating the structured calculus with existing definitions, the project successfully compiled multiple programming languages and theories, including Gallina, the language of the Coq proof assistant, and Curry-style combinators with dependent functions. The research resulting from this project has been utilized in the development of several papers, and the structured calculus itself is now an integrated part of the Coq standard library. Despite its usefulness, the project's description and definition would benefit from clearer documentation and a more comprehensive organization of its components. Moreover, several features introduced by the structured calculus remain under-exploited or difficult to utilize in the current implementation. To fully realize the calculus' potential, further development and refinement are necessary to overcome technical limitations and integrate its features more seamlessly into the Coq platform. Nonetheless, the project's contribution to the evolution of dependent function types and its successful compilation of various programming languages and theories solidify its position as a notable achievement in the field of dependent function types and programming languages with dependent types. The project's code and documentation are publicly accessible and integrated into the Coq standard library as part of the Coq version 8.15 and later releases. A challenging issue in Bayesian nonparametric mixture analysis arises when attempting to reconstruct a mixture with an unknown number of components from an ambiguous density using an uninformative Dirichlet process prior. This problem occurs because the corresponding posterior admixture weights become exchangeable and cannot be distinguished. In this research, we explore placing a Dirichlet process prior on density functions to facilitate the recovery of unique admixture weights. This is achievable by defining an uninformative prior on the random partition associated with the Dirichlet process, and we also establish the conditions under which the corresponding posterior admixture weights become non-exchangeable. A more general formulation is proposed, incorporating Dirichlet process priors on functions and weights, and we analyze the resulting model's asymptotic properties. Our method can be viewed as introducing a nonparametric constraint on the density functions to ensure distinct components, and this approach may be seen as a method for constructing stick-breaking processes that produce non-degenerate densities. We also discuss related issues and the challenges of conducting Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations for these models. A proposed algorithm exploits the properties of the Chinese restaurant process to facilitate efficient sampling. The method is demonstrated through simulations and the analysis of a real-world dataset. This research is relevant to any application where the identification of mixture components is crucial. We investigated the behavior of carbon and nitrogen within anatase TiO2 when placed in interstitial positions or substituted into the lattice. Our results, obtained through the use of a screened density functional theory, reveal key differences between these atoms when located within interstitial spaces as opposed to when they replace existing atoms. When placed in an isolated interstitial site, a carbon atom bonds with two nearby oxygen atoms, resulting in a prolonged covalent network and increased charge on the atom. In contrast, a nitrogen atom situated in an isolated interstitial location exhibits some degree of bonding with neighboring atoms but mostly exists in a more isolated state and retains a significant amount of its own electron. When substituted into the lattice, both the carbon and nitrogen atoms display a higher charge on the atom due to a lack of direct bonding with nearby atoms. The X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU) on the Athena telescope will significantly contribute to the study of turbulence in the intra-cluster medium by providing high-resolution spatial and spectral data at a moderate energy range. We have undertaken a simulation to determine the X-IFU's effectiveness in measuring the velocity field and turbulent spectrum of the intra-cluster medium. We selected several galaxy clusters with known properties and simulated X-IFU observations in the energy range 0.7-2.0 keV. The velocity field and turbulent spectrum of the intra-cluster medium were determined through an analysis of the spectral and spatial characteristics of the X-IFU data. The results showed that the X-IFU can accurately measure the velocity field and turbulent spectrum for sources with sharp edges, but may underestimate masses by a factor of two due to thermal broadening. However, in the case of sources with extended edges or diffuse structures, the X-IFU may underestimate the velocity field but overestimate the turbulent spectrum, leading to overestimation of masses. The X-IFU's effectiveness also depends on the presence of high-redshift clusters, as their cooler cores can become unresolved, leading to an overestimation of their masses. These limitations highlight the importance of joint observations with other instruments, such as spectroscopic measurements of gas temperatures, in order to fully utilize the capabilities of the X-IFU. The methodology developed in this simulation can be applied to a larger dataset of galaxy clusters, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of how the X-IFU's effectiveness changes with various observational parameters. This knowledge will be crucial in making the most out of X-IFU's observations and interpreting its results.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way, the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) is a distinct ring-like formation, encompassing a comprehensive array of molecular material. Due to its difficult observing conditions, studying the CMZ has been challenging. However, with the advent of sensitive radio telescopes like ATCA, ATLAS, and ATLAS+VORTEX have enabled detailed analysis of the chemical and physical properties of the CMZ's largest molecular cloud, the CMZ's Cloud 0 (C0). By examining 87-363 $\mu$m far-infrared images from the ATLAS and ATLAS+VORTEX data sets, a detailed study of the C0's density structure and anisotropy was conducted using the wavelet method. Analyzing the C0's density spectrum across various scales, researchers discovered a notable increase in anisotropy from a 0.1 pc to 1.0 pc scale, indicating the presence of smaller-sized filamentary structures within the C0. Additionally, an analysis of the radial distribution of the C0's density revealed a distinctive double-peak pattern, which may be attributed to the interplay between the gravitational force and the presence of the CMZ's Central Bulge. By examining various temperature maps derived from the ATLAS and ATLAS+VORRIX data sets, a distinct temperature increase was observed at the C0's core, which may be caused by the presence of early-type stars or a possible supermassive black hole at the galaxy's center. The study also discovered a weak correlation between the C0's density and temperature, suggesting that heating within the C0's core may be the result of stellar activity rather than the presence of the black hole. Consequently, this study provides new visual and spectroscopic observations, which can be compared to simulations of the CMZ's evolution to gain a deeper understanding of this intricate region of the galaxy. Furthermore, incorporating far-infrared data from the ATLAS and ATLAS+VORRIX missions will enable researchers to thoroughly examine the C0's chemistry and physical properties, offering a comprehensive perspective on this pivotal molecular cloud within the CMZ. Ultimately, this study is a significant initial step in a comprehensive analysis of the CMZ, which is critical to a comprehensive analysis of the galaxy itself. A face-scanning system that focuses on eyes offers several advantages over face-based methods, including greater freedom for users to pose, a faster detection process, and enhanced security against mask attacks. Although eye-detection technology has improved in recent years, incorporating additional facial attributes (such as the mouth) can increase detection accuracy. In this research, we introduce an innovative approach to detecting multiple facial attributes, including eyes, nose, and mouth, in both 2D and 3D dimensions. Our method utilizes a shape-aware grouping module that combines local feature detectors with geometric information to identify and connect attribute fragments in both the training and testing stages. By detecting multiple facial attributes simultaneously, our approach surpasses traditional methods that target a single attribute, such as the eye or nose. Moreover, our method's ability to perform 3D dimension predictions is a key differentiator. By regressing on the 2D predictions in a training stage called lifting, our approach predicts 3D coordinates for each attribute. We applied our eye-focused detection system to the following datasets: the 3D face dataset created for nose predictions (3DPTN), the 3D face dataset created for eye predictions (3DECI), and the 2D face attribute dataset created for general-purpose face attributes (AFAD). Our method's results on these datasets demonstrate its efficacy, as it has achieved the top performance among all submitted methods on the AFAD dataset and achieved the second-highest score on the 3DECI dataset, with the best score being obtained by a method that leverages external information. Moreover, our 3D prediction method obtained the top rating on the 3DPTN dataset, with an average error of 6.08 pixels, indicating a relatively high dimension prediction accuracy. Additionally, our method's results on the 3DECI dataset showed that it can detect a variety of eye shapes, which further supports its potential for use in eye-focused detection systems. Lastly, our method detected multiple facial attributes, including eyes, nose, and mouth, in both 2D and 3D dimensions, which makes it a comprehensive approach to facial attribute detection.

Our investigation assesses how accurately qubits and qutrits can determine mass by analyzing their response to random measurement errors. We examine the reliability of both systems under three different scenarios of measurement uncertainty, involving errors that are uncorrelated, correlated in a particular way, and completely unpredictable. Our findings show that in two out of three scenarios, qutrits outperform qubits in terms of resistance to measurement errors, while in the third scenario, qutrits actually perform worse than qubits. Interestingly, in two out of four error channels, qutrits exhibit greater precision in mass measurement than qubits, while in the other two channels, qutrits do not show an advantage. We also found that qutrits' advantage in noise tolerance is linked to their ability to distinguish between certain states that have no real-world equivalent in qubits. Moreover, our study reveals that qutrits' ability to handle errors is linked to their ability to distinguish between certain states that have no real-world equivalent in qubits. Additionally, our analysis indicates that in scenarios where qutrits outperform qubits, the difference is related to the minimum number of photons required to create qutrits and qubits, as well as the uncertainty principle. Our study could contribute to the development of error-tolerant mass measurement techniques and may have implications for the development of qutrit-based quantum technology, including communication and computation. Notably, we demonstrate that the polynomial diameter of a group is directly proportional to its conjugacy class size, providing a group characterization for finite groups with polynomial diameter in a specific degree, as well as exploring similar characteristics in nilpotent and solvable groups. Our study extends previous research by combining concepts from conjugacy classes, nilpotent subgroups, abelian subgroups, linear diameters, and Gruenberg types, offering new insights into the interconnections among these properties. This work introduces a temperature sensor designed for accuracy in measuring ambient temperature using a clock signal from a low-power CMOS oscillator. The sensor utilizes a phase-locked loop technique to determine the frequency at which the oscillator resonates in equilibrium, thus indicating the local temperature. The oscillator and temperature sensor are integrated onto a 0.18um CMOS process chip, along with a digital controller that converts the frequency into a 12-bit digital temperature reading. The sensor's accuracy is tested over a temperature range of -40degC to 120degC, showing an average error of 4.2degC and a maximum error of 11.5degC when compared to the oscillator's actual frequency. This level of inaccuracy is relatively high, possibly due to the lack of bias circuitry, but the proposed method still demonstrates the feasibility of designing accurate temperature sensors utilizing oscillator frequency. The results indicate that the proposed sensor's level of accuracy can be enhanced through the addition of bias circuitry, allowing it to meet typical sensor specifications. The design of the oscillator and temperature sensor chip was accomplished in 0.18um CMOS technology, with the oscillator operating within a frequency range of 1.5GHz to 2.8GHz and consuming an average power of 2.2mA. The addition of the temperature sensor and digital controller increased the power consumption to 6mA. The proposed sensor provides the capability to measure temperature and clock signal with the integration of the oscillator and temperature sensor onto a single chip. In stars, the magnetic field typically follows a mix of toroidal and poloidal patterns, with a stable equilibrium when these components co-exist and cancel each other out at certain points. However, maintaining this balance is challenging in stars like Ap stars and shell sparks, which have strong toroidal fields surrounded by weak poloidal fields. A recent simulation demonstrated that adding a small, stable magnetic field in the poloidal direction can amplify the star's stability. This study further explores that finding by simulating magnetic field evolution in stars using the magnetohydrodynamic equations, with parameters based on observations of the Proxima Centauri. The results show that in areas where the poloidal field is extremely weak, the toroidal field can undergo a catastrophic shift in stability. This instability is mitigated when the poloidal field is at least 1% of the toroidal field's strength. A mathematical model derived from the full magnetohydrodynamic equations confirms that the stability of the magnetic field relies on the interplay between the toroidal and poloidal components, with the latter required to be at least 10 times stronger than the former to maintain stability. This leads to the conclusion that stars with weak outer poloidal fields surrounding strong inner toroidal fields are short-term unstable. This may apply to stars like Proxima Centauri and Venus, which could explain the observed weak outer poloidal fields in these planets and stars. This study also explores how wind and magnetic diffusion affect the stability of these stars, with the results indicating that wind can prolong the stability period, while magnetic diffusion shortens it. Ultimately, this study suggests that wind plays a key role in the stability of these stars, while magnetic diffusion has a less significant effect. This could imply that wind plays a crucial part in shaping the magnetic field patterns observed in these stars and planets. This study's findings may also have implications for understanding magnetic field generation in these stars and planets. It is hypothesized that wind could be responsible for generating and maintaining the poloidal field components in these objects, a theory that could be tested through observations and simulations. Utilizing this framework, we derive a general formula for reversing the RG flow and apply it to a specific example involving a free fermion model. These definitions enable the creation of a topological stack from a extension, and vice versa, demonstrating a strong connection between extensions and stacks. This structure is locally isomorphic to the one generated by gerbes over topological stacks, and it encompasses a vast family of homotopy coherent structures, including differential crossed structures. As a result, differential crossed structures can be analyzed through the study of extensions, which provides a more flexible and coherent framework than traditional methods. Finally, this approach enables the derivation of functors related to extended structures, such as differential crossed structures, from their underlying maps. The paper's final section delves into the properties and applications of algebraic extensions, which can be viewed as a subfamily of algebraic structures over topological stacks. We examined the mass evolution of 26 molecular cores from the TeVCat sample protostar survey over a period of 12-23 years. Our analysis revealed an average mass increase of 1.3 times the dispersion per decade, with a substantial fraction of cores exhibiting rapid mass growth. This rapid growth may be a key factor in the formation of massive stars, as it can lead to the development of gravothermal fluctuations and the formation of massive protostars. However, the timescales for core formation and the availability of surrounding material will also influence the outcome of this process. Ultimately, the fate of the protostar will be determined by the competition between internal and external processes, with internal dynamics preferring the formation of massive stars, and external factors, such as nearby massive star light, tending to suppress them. This finding highlights the importance of monitoring the mass evolution of molecular cores in order to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the formation and death of massive stars. Through the study of a specific target, L1524, we discovered that the mass increase in this core is being sustained by the accumulation of dense core fragments formed as a result of the collapse of the parent cloud's density probability distribution function. This outcome highlights the complex relationships between the formation of molecular cores, the formation and disruption of dense core systems, and the formation and evolution of massive stars. Finally, with the availability of longer monitoring periods, we anticipate significant insights into the core mass function and its evolution, as well as a deeper understanding of how the formation of molecular cores is influenced by the larger scale environment. We examine the idea that work done on a system by its surroundings isn't entirely effective, instead decreasing the system's disorder and eventually becoming irrelevant. This concept of work that isn't beneficial can be seen as the average change in a system's microwork, done on the system's internal degrees of freedom, as it transitions between different microstates. Our study uses an harmonic oscillator near its ground state to illustrate this point, and we find that work that isn't beneficial is dissipated in a statistical sense, even if the system itself returns to its original state. This finding holds regardless of whether the system is at a low or high temperature. We also determine the average change in the oscillator's microwork for a single work cycle, and we find that it is directly proportional to the difference between the work done on the system and its energy lost as heat. This relationship is in line with the first law of thermodynamics. Notably, the average change in the oscillator's microwork is always negative, which indicates that the oscillator's internal structure is doing extra work on the surrounding environment over time. This phenomenon, which is a manifestation of the arrow of time, is most evident in the oscillator's highest energy levels. Ultimately, our analysis showcases the utility of using the harmonic oscillator to further understand complex systems, and it highlights the importance of recognizing the statistical nature of work done on these systems. This perspective is especially relevant in the study of quantum systems, which are often described through their microstates rather than their classical counterparts. A key challenge in neural machine translation (NMT) lies in the difficulty of balancing exploration and exploitation when generating consecutive sentences. To address this, we introduce a look-ahead attention mechanism in our proposed NMT model, allowing the decoder to attend to both the current source sentence and the previously generated target sentences. This allows our model to maintain a balance between generating conventional and sentence-level contents. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the look-ahead attention mechanism through various experiments, with notable improvements in translation accuracy and sentence-level coherence. Our method achieves particularly significant gains in InDomain data settings and showcases robust performance across multiple evaluation metrics and languages. Our code is openly available at https://github.com/ghrua/laa-nmt.

In monitoring and managing urban road conditions, sensors are crucial for accuracy, but they are often limited in number due to high deployment costs. This research explores how ridesourcing vehicles can enhance sensing reliability and coverage in urban areas by regularly traveling between starting points and destinations. We develop a mathematical model to optimize the placement of these vehicles for best sensing results. The problem is complex because their movement patterns intersect and overlap, making it difficult to define coverage areas and predict data reliability. To tackle this challenge, we create a discrete grid to divide the city into areas and assign scores to each one based on its sensing reliability. The total score can be maximized through a vehicle seeding strategy. This approach is tested on a simulated city and compared to random placement methods, yielding notable improvements in reliability and coverage, along with reduced coordination overhead. Furthermore, we investigate how different city sizes, traffic patterns, and sensor scoring systems affect the vehicle placement strategy. The results provide valuable insights into the effectiveness of ridesourcing-based sensing and its potential applications in real-world city management scenarios. This research paves the way for future numerical methods and experimental implementations. The developed framework, along with evaluation metrics and simulation tools, is available open-source for further exploration and optimization techniques. Upcoming work will focus on adapting this model to optimize vehicle placement in real-world settings with changing traffic patterns and road conditions. This research introduces a new variable stepsize Signal-to-Noise Ratio Estimation using the Generalized Method of Moments (SGLM) and adapts it for use on nonuniform sampling schedules. By modifying the formulation to account for the specific sampling times, the estimated SNR is optimized to match the corresponding true SNR. A key differentiation between this method and its constant and linear stepsize counterparts is the generation of unbiased estimators for the second-order moments. Multi-line spectral series analysis is a complex problem that requires the identification of several concurrent one-dimensional spectra. This task is often resolved with the interlace method, which separates and reconstructs the spectra through their superimposition. However, the interlace method assumes a fixed structure for all line series, which is not always the case. In this research, a new approach called MFSSA is introduced, allowing for the simultaneous analysis of multiple line series with varying architectures. This method is based on the combination of Fourier transforms and sliding windows, enabling it to handle both simple and complex spectral patterns. Furthermore, MFSSA includes an innovative strategy for determining the architecture of individual line series. This approach uses the results from the main analysis and reconstructs the specific line series through the separation of the entire spectrum. Consequently, MFSSA is an adaptable method that is capable of solving a wide range of multi-line series analysis problems. It can be applied to various real-world scenarios, such as the analysis of temperature curves, remote sensing images, or glycosyl-fragment spectra, ultimately leading to more accurate assignments of molecular structures. In addition, a publicly available MFSSA software package has been developed as part of the XWASSER program, making it easier for users without advanced mathematical background to utilize the method. The program includes an intuitive graphical user interface and is compatible with multiple operating systems. To demonstrate the capabilities of MFSSA, it was applied to the analysis of two remote sensing images containing superimposed spectra, resulting in the identification of up to 200 distinct components in a single observation. This showcases the method's ability to handle a large number of line series with complex architectures and sets the stage for its utilization in the analysis of glycosyl-fragment spectra. Although the method has been demonstrated with a one-dimensional Discrete Fourier Transform, it is also suitable for two-dimensional NMR spectra following the application of appropriate processing techniques. The innovative approach of combining sliding windows and Fourier transforms makes MFSSA an adaptable method for the analysis of multiple line series with varying architectures, enabling it to successfully tackle complex problems in various domains. This has the potential to lead to more accurate assignments of molecular structures in areas like glycosyl-fragment spectra. The publicly available MFSSA software package, part of the XWASSER program, makes it easier for users without an advanced mathematical background to utilize the method and showcases its capabilities on remote sensing images containing superimposed spectra, resulting in the identification of up to 200 distinct components in a single observation.

The paper investigates a random walk with i.i.d. components that have the same mean of zero. It re-examines the asymptotic behavior of the walk's increments, particularly in the tail region, and identifies conditions under which the walk's asymptotic distribution can be classified into one of three categories, depending on the value of a parameter 'b' that measures the tail thickness of the distribution of the walk's increments. If 'b' is greater than one, the walk's asymptotic distribution follows a fractal pattern; if 'b' is equal to one, the distribution is a mixture of a heavy-tailed component and a negligible light-tailed component; if 'b' is less than one, the distribution is dominated by a heavy-tailed component; if 'b' is equal to zero, the walk's asymptotic distribution has the same properties as the standard random walk; and if 'b' is greater than zero, the walk's asymptotic distribution has a different structure that is characterized by an alpha-stable distribution with a heavy-tailed component and a negligible light-tailed component. The study further explores the relationship between the walk's asymptotic distribution and its spectral density function. It also analyzes conditions under which the walk's components share the same distribution as the standard random walk, and discusses the limitations of existing results in the field. Finally, the paper presents two applications of the investigated problems: one related to autoregressive processes and the other to random walks with time-dependent components. The study also proposes a new estimator for the best predictor of a random variable, and investigates its properties in the context of heavy-tailed components. The results are validated through Monte Carlo simulations, and the study also provides an overview of the related open problems in the field. The study is based on the previous research by Mandelbrot and Van Ness (1968), and it is intended to provide a comprehensive analysis of the random walk model with i.i.d. components that have the same mean of zero. The study is also based on the previous research by Taqqu (1977) and it is intended to provide a more detailed analysis of the asymptotic distribution of the walk's increments than the previous studies. The study is conducted in the context of the fractional Brownian motion with a non-integral Hurst exponent, and it is intended to provide the conditions under which the walk's asymptotic distribution can be classified into one of the three categories, depending on the value of the Hurst exponent. Optimizing plasma sources is crucial for plasma applications and can be achieved by fine-tuning electron temperature and density. Knowing the source's spatial and temporal characteristics is essential but often difficult to measure directly. This study demonstrates the usefulness of spectroscopically analyzing light scattering from plasmas, a method initially proposed by McWhirer in 1964. The approach is mathematically detailed, including how to calculate relevant spectral lines and determine essential plasma properties. The proposed method's effectiveness is tested through numerical simulations, which show it can accurately determine key parameters even with limited spectral resolution, provided the observation angle is optimal. The best results are obtained when observing right across the plasma surface, minimizing the impact of source size and shape, and yielding accurate measurements of temperature, density, and their spatial extent along the line of sight. The proposed method can also handle time-dependent situations by analyzing successive spectra, which may require further experimental configuration for accurate data collection. To validate the theoretical predictions, the proposed method is applied to numerical data representing a specific plasma source, similar to one created by demountable mirrors in particle beam systems. The results indicate a high degree of accuracy, with a temperature determination of 0.1 eV and a density determination of 10^10 particles per volume. The method could benefit the development and analysis of plasma sources, making it suitable for a wide range of applications that rely on plasma, including material processing, medical technology, and scientific research tools. Furthermore, this approach may also be adapted for use with other spectroscopic techniques and could be a valuable teaching tool for understanding plasma and its applications. Additionally, the influence of changing plasma parameters on spectroscopic patterns could be explored to support the development of plasma source optimization methods. The proposed method is now available online as an interactive visualization tool accompanied by its source code in the form of a Python package that can be used from a command line or integrated into custom applications via a graphical user interface. The code enables users to calculate the expected spectral lines for various plasma sources and provide a comprehensive analysis of the resulting spectra, thus making it an invaluable resource for both fundamental research and technology development. The code is fully compatible with a wide range of operating systems, including Windows, Linux, and macOS, and can be executed in various computational environments. The code is also available on GitHub, along with a sample manual that explains its use in detail. The proposed method is anticipated to contribute meaningfully to the advancement of plasma sources and their numerous applications. The hamiltonian path index (HPI) of a graph H is defined as the minimum number of hamiltonian paths required to cover all vertices of H. In this study, we examine the hamhamiltonian path index of two specific types of graphs: powers of cycles and powers of trees. We aim to establish a connection between the hamiltonian path index and hamiltonian number of these graphs. Specifically, we wish to determine the minimum number of hamiltonian paths necessary to cover a graph that is a power of a cycle or a tree, and compare this to the hamiltonian number of the same graph. This research may lead to a better understanding of how hamiltonian paths and hamiltonian cycles within a graph are related, and could potentially provide guidance on determining the hamiltonian number through hamhamiltonian path index. We present theoretical limitations and computational results for powers of cycles and trees. We observe that in many cases, the hamhamiltonian path index is equal to the hamiltonian number of the graph, and note that this research can be applied to various types of graphs, including those in three dimensions. However, no general formula can be applied to all powers of cycles or trees. We also note that determining the hamhamiltonian path index of a graph is computationally complex, and may require significant time and memory for larger graphs. We propose a new branch and bound algorithm to efficiently determine the hamhamiltonian path index of a graph, and demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm through our theoretical and computational results. The source code for this algorithm is available online. We hope that this algorithm can be applied to a broader range of graphs, and contribute to the field of hamiltonian path index research. In an attempt to slow COVID-19's spread, many countries imposed restrictive non-pharmaceutical policies, however these measures come with significant economic and social costs. A potential intermediate step involves finding an existing anti-inflammatory treatment that can reduce COVID-19 mortality and severities, thus minimizing the need for strict lockdowns. This would require such treatments to act quickly, possibly by inhibiting cell death's propagation through a feedback loop. Given available data, we model the amplification of lung tissue damage caused by COVID-19 in relation to a host's immune response. Our analysis suggests that only anti-inflammatory drugs able to reach the lungs rapidly can be effective, and even then, may only delay the progression to full tissue damage, not halt it completely. This finding is consistent with observed results from clinical trials and studies, and highlights the importance of considering the transport of substances within the body when evaluating potential therapies. Furthermore, our model highlights the potential risks of cytotoxic cell death acceleration due to the overproduction of certain chemicals, and suggests that targeting the loop driving cell death's spread, especially in areas with inadequate immune response, may yield more effective treatments. We also provide a framework for incorporating additional information into the model, and utilize this framework to explore the effects of different treatment delivery methods, such as inhaled anti-inflammatory drugs, on the progression of lung tissue damage caused by COVID-19. This research is part of an ongoing effort to address the global health crisis caused by the pandemic through mathematical modeling and analysis. The model developed here is particularly relevant to the discussion on potential therapeutic uses of anti-inflammatory drugs outlined in the preface to the report. We propose an algorithm that discovers exogenous variables affecting the state transition dynamics from observations and reinforcement learning data. Unlike existing methods, our approach leverages policy updates to inform its search, unlike alternative approaches. The proposed algorithm is based on the premise that changes in policy reflections can indicate the presence of external factors, thus, it excels in discovering variables with short detection periods. Our method uses the anticipated changes resulting from policy adjustments to guide its search for external variables. A analysis of the algorithm's properties is provided, alongside experimental results illustrating its ability to identify multiple relevant variables in a variety of scenarios. We've created a new verification tool called HELMHOLTZ, which verifies Michelson programs used in Tezos smart contracts and demonstrates its effectiveness on various contract vulnerabilities. VERDIER, another verification tool, laid the groundwork for this development. However, Michelson's combination of strictly-typed values and operational behavior, along with its batched and effectful computations, presented significant challenges for a reliable and accurate verification tool like HELMHOLTZ. To tackle these difficulties, we've made substantial contributions, particularly in verifying function calls and the effects of computations, which have enabled HELMHOLTZ to successfully verify complex contracts, even in situations where traditional tools like VERDIER fail. Furthermore, HELMHOLTZ has verified several real-world contracts, including some that were later found to be vulnerable and were repaired with its aid. To ensure the reliability of HELMHOLTZ, we've conducted extensive testing and performed comparisons with other verification tools. Our experience has highlighted both the strengths and limitations of Michelson's design and suggested possible improvements, such as verifying function calls by verifying the interaction between functions and their environments rather than individual functions in isolation. Additionally, we propose a new approach to verifying the computational steps of Michelson programs, which could be applied to other languages as well. This new approach involves verifying the relationship between programs and their effects on the basis of program steps rather than individual steps in isolation. As a result, we believe HELMHOLTZ represents an important step towards creating more secure and versatile smart contracts and can serve as a model for the verification of similar programs used in other blockchain platforms. To facilitate further development, we're releasing HELMHOLTZ as an open-source tool. Its verification capabilities can be activated via the 'heli' command-line option followed by'verify', and it's compatible with Michelson programs version 6 and later. Users can activate the SMT solver Z3 for HELMHOLTZ via the 'heli' command-line option followed by 'z3'. Moreover, we're making the source code and the specifications for the verified programs and contracts publicly available on the GitLab repository https://gitlab.com/tezos/ahvm-helmholtz. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for analyzing complex graph-structured data. Despite their effectiveness, there's still a significant challenge in tuning the training parameters for GCNs. This problem is addressed by introducing a novel framework called MetaLearn-GCN, which utilizes a meta-learning approach to develop a generalizable trainer network that can effectively train various GCN models with minimal loss of performance. This meta-trainer network is capable of adapting to different dataset conditions through a few samples, which is equivalent to achieving optimal training with an infinite number of steps. The key components of this meta-trainer network are a parameterizer and an optimizerizer, which are represented by combining multiple GCN modules with linear optimizer components. The meta-trainer network is trained through a series of MetaLearn stages before being applied to adapt to new datasets in Adapation stages. The experimental results show that this meta-trainer network is capable of achieving optimal training performance on par with that of highly tuned, custom-trained networks for both node classification and graph classification tasks. The source code of this meta-trainer network has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/MetaLearn-GCN. The data used in the experiments is available at https://github.com/ghrua/MetaLearn-GCN/blob/main/data.md. The code for visualizing the adaptation process is based on torch-vis library, which can be found at https://github.com/ghrua/MetaLearn-GCN/blob/main/visualize.md. The paper associated with this code has been published in the 13th ACM International Conference on Web Search and Data Mining, where the full paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04352. The code has been tested on a system with an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU. The project is hosted on https://github.com/ghrua/MetaLearn-GCN. Formally verifying the implementation of safety-critical systems involves comparing their actual behavior to their intended behavior as described in pseudocodes. However, existing pseudocodes fall short in ensuring the correctness and safety of implementations. This is because traditional pseudocodes are written in an informal style that is easy to understand for humans but difficult to analyze computationally. To address this limitation, the concept of logical pseudocodes was introduced as a medium for formal verification. However, the current approach to generating logical pseudocodes is inefficient as it requires a significant amount of additional work. This research proposes a novel framework that allows for the conversion of traditional pseudocodes written in while-loops into their logical equivalents, thereby streamlining the formal verification process. This framework is particularly useful in analyzing the termination of systems that rely on recursive protocols. As an example of its applications, our method is utilized in conjunction with the Kastenbaum-Lamport protocol to display its potential termination. This demonstrates the capabilities of our method in validating the termination properties of systems composed of distributed components. The protocol in question exhibits its potential termination through a logical pseudocode that can be validated computationally. This, in turn, enables the analysis of its potential termination in relation to the system's component timeouts. Furthermore, our method is adaptable to any while-loop based pseudocode, making it a versatile tool for the formal verification process. This research proposal is the foundation for a proposed PhD course of study at the University of Oxford. The underlying methods have been proven viable in several previous studies, albeit in more limited contexts. The key contribution of this research is the development of a general-purpose method for converting traditional pseudocodes into their logical equivalents, thereby streamlining the formal verification process. Our approach uses $O(k\cdot poly(log k, log n))$ dimensions and produces a coreset with $k^{2k}$ points, requiring only a single pass through the data. In large-scale grid worlds, complex scenarios can be broken down into simpler components called superstates that capture the underlying dynamics. We introduce a method to automatically generate partitions for these scenarios, enabling effective planning by incorporating a cost function that considers future state predictions. Specifically, in pursuit-evasion scenarios, our approach divides the grid into superstates that guide a mobile robot in continuously avoiding an evader until they meet at a specific location or until the evader reaches a designated target. Through numerous examples and testing with a built-in planner, our method demonstrates success in creating meaningful partitions, leading to the evasion of the evader for an arbitrarily long time. Furthermore, our approach results in predictable future state predictions, ensuring safe and effective operation in these scenarios. We demonstrate the benefits of our method through comparative analyses against alternative division strategies. The source code and accompanying data for our research are available online.

The concept of rotating halo nuclei with complex, deformed configurations poses a significant challenge for existing understanding. Research has shown that rotating nuclei within the actinide region, particularly in berkelium and gold, exhibit unusual patterns of energy based on the central body and peripheral regions. To investigate this phenomenon, our team has conducted a comprehensive analysis of measurements obtained from nuclear recoil technique and excitation functions for low-spin states in $^{257}$No and $^{258}$No. Our research has led to the development of a rotating halo model, which consists of an central body spinning rapidly while attached to a slowly rotating peripheral shell. According to our findings, the densities of 0+-1 and 2+-1 states in 257No and 258No are similar, which provides insight into the influence of core softness. Additionally, a comparison between theoretical predictions obtained from finite model space calculations and our results has provided further evidence for the rotating halo model, which may be applicable to other nuclei within the actinide region. This study has resulted in a new concept of rotating halo nuclei, which offers a fresh perspective on the understanding of complex nuclear configurations. Recently, video super-resolution has achieved significant progress through the use of video swin transformers. A major restriction of existing research lies in their exclusive focus on single-frame inputs, which neglects the rich information within videos. This overlook has resulted in the development of methods that rely on elaborate propagation schemes to exploit temporal richness. In this study, we propose a efficient and straightforward way to leverage temporal information for video super-resolution. The proposed BasicVSR++ model incorporates a novel temporal block that is characterized by a lightweight and lightweight spatial transformer. This innovative design enables efficient temporal information exploration, achieving a 1.8 times increase in efficiency and a 1.3 times improvement in PSNR compared to the prominent PIVSR model. Moreover, the proposed method exhibits exceptional adaptability when applied to various scaling factors and displays excellent practical applicability, demonstrating superior performance in real-world scenarios. Our code and model have been made publicly available on GitHub and MMKV Repository. Our work has been openly shared on arXiv.

When applying a single dynamics model to multiple reinforcement learning tasks, using an optimal policy may not be effective due to the model's inherent limitations, leading to a phenomenon we've experienced firsthand in our own experiments. This issue motivates the search for a different approach. By leveraging multiple learned dynamics models, we can develop a corresponding set of optimal policies, but this method is inefficient as it requires the most resources to achieve the best results. An alternative strategy involves selecting the best-performing policy based on online sampling data, but this method is slow and impractical in complex scenarios. In our work, we propose an alternative method that involves dividing the task division problem into two layers: a higher layer responsible for managing the overall strategy, and a lower layer managing daily operations based on individual models. This method achieves a balance between efficiency and performance by monte carlo sampling across sub-policies within defined action spaces, only occasionally updating the higher-layer strategy through offline data analysis. Our method succeeds in maintaining a level of optimality, and the associated algorithm has a proven convergence rate. In our experiments, our approach demonstrates superior performance in multi-task reinforcement learning scenarios, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. The associated code is available on an open-source platform famous for its ease of use.

A well-known challenge in selecting a balanced sample for statistical analysis is the exponential time complexity of the Largest Minimum (LM) problem when the dataset is presented in an unordered form. To address this challenge, a new algorithm has been developed that runs in linear time complexity and enables the efficient identification of a balanced sample within a random subset of the dataset. This algorithm utilizes a hash table to store the minimum values associated with each unique feature and can be applied to a limited set of features. It essentially simplifies the LM problem by reducing the feature complexity from linear to constant, enabling the implementation of a simple and efficient large minimum algorithm that runs in O(n) time complexity. It is demonstrated that this algorithm can effectively handle large datasets by selecting a balanced sample of a random subset of 100 million data points. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through a real-world example, with results showing that it can select a balanced sample with a high degree of accuracy. It is also shown that this algorithm can be safe from adversarial attacks, as proven through a game theoretic analysis. It is noteworthy that this algorithm can be applied to a limited set of features; however, this limitation can be mitigated through incremental processing. We've conducted multiple-frequency radio and millimeter wave observations of the binary pulsar system PSR B1133+16, identifying multiple scattering screens between the Earth and the pulsar, totaling seven, along with two screen complexes within the system containing its companion star and surrounding environment. By utilizing our recent phase screen model incorporated into the PRESTO and RADAGAST pulsar signal processing software packages, we've obtained accurate TOAs at 1.7 GHz across 630 days, achieving a fit quality of $\chi^2_{\nu}=1.31$, and detected magnetic vector field orientation swings relative to the companion star, occurring over 678 days. Our study reveals the star's influence on the pulsar's electromagnetic field, including rotation-powered vacuum pulses, and offers implications for pulse profile polarization analysis. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate the capability of highly sensitive, multi-frequency pulsar searches to provide accurate TOAs, ultimately contributing to tests of gravitational theories with pulsars. Our research was conducted using the Arecibo radio telescope observations from 2018 to 2020, and the study's results are available on the pulsar catalog webpage. We also present a hypothesis regarding the possibility of detecting light curves from the companion star of PSR B1133+16 during its upcoming eclipse.

Annotating text documents on a large scale is an essential task in natural language processing, and typically involves a large team of annotators working manually. To enhance their productivity, introduce consistency across annotations and standardize the quality, we propose a system called CoAnno. This system utilizes a web-based interface and enables multiple users to collaborate on the annotation of a single document. Within the system, a team can create and manage their own tasks, track progress, maintain quality control measures, and even provide training data for machine learning models. A total of eight users from two groups participated in a usability study using the CoAnno system. The results show the benefits of collaborative annotation, standardizing quality across annotations, and providing ongoing training for the annotators. The design of the main interface and specific features of the system was evaluated through both a user satisfaction survey and a usability analysis. The data collected indicated a high level of user satisfaction with the design, along with several key areas for improvement and several successful implementations of the system's machine learning training data. A total of 2 million words of text were annotated using the CoAnno system as part of the study. The system, including the code and data collected, has been openly shared on the GitHub platform. Our study examines zero-energy peaks resulting from non-Majorana effects in proximized nanowire devices, focusing on their temperature-driven shifts and changes. We develop a full quantum treatment, accounting for temperature-related broadening and zero-bias peak analysis, to investigate the interplay between Majorana and Ohmic terminals. Our findings show that at finite temperatures, the zero-energy peak's behavior is significantly influenced by a competition between two mechanisms. Firstly, temperature induces a shift in the peak position from $\Delta$ to zero due to the fermionic distribution function, albeit this shift is constrained by the Majorana binding energy and may be obscured by the device's thermal broadening. Secondly, temperature can trigger a peak splitting at certain conditions, leading to the emergence of a zero-broadened peak at the new gap energy. This peak splitting is driven by a combination of the Majorana gap and the Fermi distribution function, and can be broadened out of existence by increasing the temperature further. The duration of peak splitting before the broadening takes over is exponentially lengthened as the temperature decreases, aligning with expectations based on the Majorana gap by tunnel decay theory. The duration of peak splitting can be adjusted by modifying the charge, albeit in a more minimal manner. The proposed model predicts that a substantial increase in zero-broadened peaks can be achieved through a combination of highly low temperatures and finely tuned device parameters, thereby potentially enabling unambiguous identification of the Majorana zero-mode. Furthermore, our study provides a framework for interpreting experimental outcomes in the context of the interplay between Majorana and ohmic terminals and suggests that temperature may serve as a decisive factor in uncovering the existence of zero-mode peaks. The associated discussion offers several experimentally feasible paths for validating our findings, including variations in voltage, temperature, and the application of external magnetic fields, as well as considerations for optimizing device performance in the presence of lattices and other factors. Ultimately, our study emphasizes the significance of accounting for temperature and related broadening in the analysis of zero-energy peaks to ensure an accurate understanding of the underlying physics at play. The proposed method for analyzing zero-broadened peaks also opens up avenues for exploring new aspects of the field. The code allows users to visualize the influence of a range of parameters, including temperature, Fermi energy, tunnel coupling, magnetic field, and lattice size on zero-energy peak profiles. We introduce VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS), a comprehensive sound source localization benchmark consisting of 13,485 video sources with accurate labels, used to evaluate the ability of autonomous agents to recognize sources of sound. This benchmark, drawing from a diverse range of sources including the VGG-Sound dataset, incorporates various categories of objects, animal sounds, and human actions, as well as diverse backgrounds and environments. To create it, we modified the existing VGG-Sound dataset to fit the requirements of sound source localization, adding specific markers to indicate the origin of sounds within each video. Unlike other available datasets, our benchmark does not rely on manual annotations or assume access to additional information beyond the sounds themselves. It focuses exclusively on the ability of autonomous agents to recognize sources of sound, making it more suitable for use in the development of self-localizing autonomous agents. To demonstrate the value of this benchmark, we trained and tested a simple sound source localization model on it, achieving impressive results and demonstrating the potential for this approach to contribute to the development of more effective self-localization methods. We introduce the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), an innovative new model that enhances hyperbolic graph convolutional networks (H-GCNs) by utilizing the Lorentzian distance instead of the Jacobi distance. The Lorentzian distance is a more natural metric for Euclidean spaces beyond the sphere. By leveraging this distance metric, LGCN learns a more accurate and robust node feature representation than existing H-GCNs. Additionally, the Lorentzian distance allows for the derivation of an efficient gradient computation method, making LGCN's training process much faster than other H-GCNs while achieving similar or better performance. Our model also introduces a novel closed-form expression for the Lorentzian distance between two points on a sphere, which serves as a key contribution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LGCN through comprehensive experiments on a range of classification tasks, including the Euclidean graph-based Charles River Labs toxicity dataset, the hyperbolic graph-based face-scene dataset, and a set of synthetic datasets. Our results show that LGCN outperforms other H-GCNs or matches their performance while reducing training time. The code for the Lorentzian graph convolutional network is openly available on GitHub.

We utilize the paramagnon theory to analyze spin-orbit coupling in transition metal oxides, considering their electronic properties as described by the dynamical mean-field theory. This allows us to investigate how spin-orbit coupling relates to interaction effects and crystal field splitting within these materials. By applying this theory to the case of Sr$_2$FeMoO$_6$, we develop a simplified expression for spin-orbit coupling and calculate its average value in the material. Our results show that spin-orbit coupling in Sr$_2$FeMoO$_6$ can be significant, potentially exceeding 100 meV, and may influence the material's magnetic properties, leading to a combination of isolated and weakly coupled effective SISO models depending on the crystallographic arrangement. This may be relevant to the understanding of magnetic properties in strained samples of this material. Our method can also be applied to other ferromagnetic transition metal oxides with strong correlations and large crystal field splitting.

By examining the properties of these relative $I$-functions, we establish their orthogonality and positivity. Moreover, we demonstrate that the relative $I$-functions can be used to express linear combinations of Schur functions, thereby connecting them to the fundamental periodicity of $I$-functions. This paper delves into the potential risks of generative adversarial networks (GANs) misrepresenting medical conditions, specifically when their underlying code can be easily altered. We demonstrate that, given a generative model trained on x-rays, an adversary can devise a method to manipulate the latent code and fool the model into producing misleading diagnoses for undetected fractures, even if the original image didn't contain such fractures. Our findings highlight the importance of exploring safety precautions for GANs in the limited and imbalanced medical imaging datasets commonly encountered. We illustrate the admissibility of this concern through an experiment involving a synthetic dataset, and subsequently apply the same approach to a real-world dataset containing chest x-rays. We have developed a novel approach to determine the best-fitting approximation over a given mesh element, significantly increasing the method's versatility. Our studies demonstrate that this method yields highly accurate approximations, with manageable computational costs, as evidenced by the optimal $O(N^2)$ complexity for assembling a single element. This innovative approach offers an efficient and accurate way to approximate a wide variety of functions while also providing a robust tool for developing new numerical methods.
